Mr. Chairman, I wish to take only a few minutes of the time of the committee in order to air a grievance or a problem that I have. Quite frankly, I do not know where to go with it, except here. I wish to appeal a decision made by treasury board. I have made inquiries around parliament hill but I really have not found anyone yet who can tell me exactly what a member can do in a situation such as this, where treasury board has made a decision and one wants to appeal it.
This question concerns the raising of the rentals of the crown owned dwellings in the village of Ralston, Alberta. The Department of National Defence, which is indirectly involved in this matter, tell me it is not in their hands at all because there was an order, or a directive which came from treasury board that these rentals should be brought in line with some standard that prevails. I disagree with this standard. In any event, I cannot get any satisfactory answer from the Department of National Defence. The defence research board of the Department of National Defence claim that they are in the same position, that treasury board has issued this directive, or order, and they therefore have no power to rescind it or do anything about it.
This village is some 30 miles from a city. It is therefore that distance from doctors, dentists, markets and most other community services that are right at hand for dwellings inside a city. I think this is something that should be taken into consideration. I wish to put on the record the answer to a question asked about this matter. This answer is to be found in Hansard of June 12, at which time I asked:
What was the total cost of constructing the crown owned residences in the village of Ralston, Alberta?
The answer was "$1,694,789". The second part of that question was:
What is the total amount of rent collected on these residences?
The answer I received was "$10,769 per month". I wanted to know what was the total rent collected on these residences from the time they were built, to see whether the

government had recovered most of its capital investment through rental. But the government did not answer it in that way, so I had to do some calculating myself. I find that even at the old levels of rent, before the raise came along they were collecting $10,769 a month, as I said, which amounts to about $130,000 a year. I happen to know that many of these residences have been in place and have been earning rent for the government for 13 years or more. At this rental figure it would take almost exactly 13 years for the government to recover all its capital investment in them. Therefore the government had no justifiable reason whatever for increasing the rents effective August 1 this year. In some cases the increase in rental was as much as 94 per cent, all at once. If the government were to tell us how much they have collected in rentals over these years, I think we would see that almost all their investment has been recovered, and they are therefore making what might be termed an unconscionable profit on the rentals now being charged. In spite of this they have raised all the rents. As I said, in one case at least the increase was as much as 94 per cent.
The grievance I have is with treasury board. I appeal to them to rescind this order raising the rentals, because there is no apparent justification for it; and in any event the increase is too much. I also disagree, if that is the right word, with the method used to evaluate what the rentals should be. I am told they sent an inspector from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to assess these buildings and establish a fair rental for them, but he took the general area into consideration. Certainly, if they were in the city of Medicine Hat the rents these people are now charged following the raise would not be more than that being collected commercially, if I may call it that, for houses of the same size and with the same accommodation right in the city. But they are not in the city; they are 30 miles out. I believe that a low rent in this village could be considered as one of the legitimate fringe benefits to people living there who have to commute back and forth 30 miles to doctors, dentists, market facilities and most other community services.
That is all I wish to say on this matter, Mr. Chairman. This is a grievance I have had for the last three or four months, and I seem to run right up against a stone wall in trying to find in the government anyone who will even take this question back to treasury board and have them consider it.

Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity to draw to the attention of

the government certain points which, in my opinion, are of vital importance to our areas and eastern Canada.
I would like to draw the attention of the hon. members and of the representatives of the federal Department of Agriculture to very serious problems which I already raised many times during this session. I did say "the representatives of the federal Department of Agriculture"; these hon. members do not realize, it seems, that the onus lies upon them as representatives elected by the people to give to their department instructions which would help to settle the many problems facing farmers in eastern Canada, in my province and in the maritimes, as well as in the eastern part of Ontario.
The house will remember that on October 15 last I made a stand against the millions of dollars lost by our farmers and especially those in the dairy industry in the province of Quebec.
I regret that there are no members of the government from eastern Canada, no responsible ministers in this field now in the house. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) is still absent today and I deplore the fact that the Minister without Portfolio and his parliamentary secretary are also absent.
I especially wish to call the attention of the government on the millions of dollars that farmers in my province and in eastern Canada lose now because the new government policy was put forward too early, was not considered carefully, with the result that at present, our farmers received much less money than last year. Indeed, it should be the reverse as the prices of dairy products are higher than they were last year.
I should like to emphasize another point-* and my comments will only take a short time -that is equally important to eastern Canada's agriculturists. I am referring to feed.
It seems to me that since last April, the government has had enough time to draft proper legislation. Besides, legislation had already been drafted by the previous government, which would have been favourable to eastern growers as well as to those in my province.
This question is a very important one. At the present time, the prices of feed are too high. The growers of my province and those of the east cannot make any profits. Therefore, it is the duty of the government to take adequate action as soon as possible.
As I mentioned earlier, I say again that, in my opinion, the Minister of Agriculture could easily draft legislation to authorize farmers, flour mills and co-operatives of eastern Canada to organize themselves into a purchasing board in order to buy the feed they need

Interim Supply
directly from the Canadian wheat board, so as to secure their supplies at favourable prices during a period of from eight to ten months.
\ should also like to call the attention of the government on the point made in their brief by the Cooperative federee and the united farmers of Canada, to the effect that the federal Minister of Agriculture should like the government to consider the matter and submit a report as soon as possible so that when we go back to our respective provinces and ridings, we may tell our farmers that we are looking after their problems.
My third point has to do with a question I put to the Minister of Agriculture last June. When I asked whether the government intended to appoint a vice president within the Farm Credit Corporation, the minister replied that the question was under advisement. The matter has been under consideration since last June and it is well known that the corporation will loan over $100 million to Canadian farmers this year.
In my opinion, the Minister of Agriculture should make such an appointment immediately so that some will look after the interests of Canadian farmers in general.
Since I am on the subject of farm credit, I should like to say a few words in that connection. Last Sunday evening, I listened to a program on television where the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) stated that only 109 loans were granted in the province of Quebec last year.
Subsequently, he asked the people to deny that fact. As a matter of fact, last year, in the province of Quebec, 804 loans were granted for a total amount of $11,434,700. This is a far cry from the 109 loans mentioned by the hon. member for Lapointe.
I should also like to refer to the building of a bridge between Three Rivers and Ste. Angele, in my riding. I hope that the Minister of Transport will soon be in a position to inform the house that the government supports the legislation carried by the Conservative government on March 4, 1963, so as to remove any doubts among my constituents who have been looking forward to the construction of this bridge for several years. It is high time it was built.
The Minister of Transport should necessarily face up to his responsibilities and say: "Well, the bridge will be built."
I would also like to discuss the new legislation granting a $500 premium for housing construction during wintertime. A $500 premium is paid for each dwelling; so if the house includes four units, a $2,000 premium is paid. But when the house has four units and an additional one in the basement, then no premium is paid.

I had understood, as many taxpayers in my constituency did, that the maximum was $2,000 and that if the house being built contained five or six units, the limit was a maximum of $2,000; but after explanations from the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen); we found the situation is entirely different.
If the house being built contains five units, the owner receives absolutely nothing, whereas if the house being built contains four units, the owner will receive $2,000. I wonder whether there would be some means of improving markedly the provisions of that legislation. I am of the opinion it would be wise to allow those persons who build five housing units, one of which is in the basement, to benefit from this maximum premium of $2,000.
The last point I want to raise in this debate on interim supply concerns federal-provincial relations. You recall that, before the election on April 8 of this year, at a time when there was a Conservative government in office in Ottawa, the premier of the province of Quebec delivered an ultimatum. We were not the ones to use that word, the premier himself did in a televised broadcast. As a matter of fact, to a reporter who asked him:
Do you consider that part of your speech on the budget which refers to the increase in taxsharing to 25-25-100, as an ultimatum?
Mr. Lesage answered yes.
And according to an editorial published last November 23 in La Reforme, the official organ of the Quebec Liberal federation, it was indeed an ultimatum on the part of Mr. Lesage.
Today, we are entitled to ask ourselves whether Mr. Lesage would still have delivered his ultimatum to the federal government, prior to last April 8, if the Liberal party had been in office. As a matter of fact, during the election campaign, they said that the Grits had to be in power in Ottawa and at Quebec. And now that this is exactly the situation in which they find themselves, they feel the ultimatum no longer exists.
It was thought that ultimatum from the province of Quebec was to be taken seriously. But it is found that such is not the case. In fact, if you have a quick look around the house, you will see that the ministers from my province and all the other members, except the few that are here, have probably gone to meet Mr. Lesage to tell him: Do not feel sad, we will maintain at least the prestige of the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, the governments which, before 1940, succeeded each other in the province of Quebec-the Liberal as well as the Union Nationale governments-always fought

for the province's autonomy. But, unfortunately, during the war the Liberal government in Quebec and the Liberal government in Ottawa agreed to deprive that province of its taxing powers, while promising to give them back when the war was over.
Afterwards, the Quebec government fought unceasingly to recover its taxation rights yielded to the federal government. We need those fiscal rights because we want to carry through our education system which comes under the sole jurisdiction of the provinces.
We need these taxation rights to look after our highway system which comes under the sole jurisdiction of the provinces.
Moreover, we need these taxation rights because provincial responsibilities are forever increasing. We need the necessary funds to meet our ever increasing responsibilities and fulfil other commitments entered upon in every field.
Before closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I merely wish to say that several times in this house I heard members make speeches with which I did not agee. But I want every member who sits here, from whatever province he may come and to whatever party he may belong, to be able to talk freely and say what he really thinks.
I listened the other day to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). I liked his speech, not because I accept or approve what he said, but because I saw a member stand up and say what he really thinks. Even if we do not agree with the hon. member, we must act like gentlemen and let him speak freely, and perhaps do the same ourselves later on. I also read the speech which an hon. Liberal member made the other day in Toronto, and though I do not at all agree with what he said, he at least fully expressed his views, and that is what all those who represent various ridings here in this federal parliament, should do. And when we are gentlemanly enough to accept the fact that each hon. member may rise to express his views- in short, speak as he thinks fit-then the dialogue will start and we may say with some truth that in Canada, we are able to know what others think and to express our own thoughts.
Therefore we should stop whining whenever a member from another party and another part of Canada rises to say something with which we may not agree. If he is a member from Quebec, we have something to say about the views expressed by other members, and, if the member is from another province, he may object to our ideas. Well, we want all hon. members to be able to speak freely, and then we shall be able to reply and to air our own views. The only 28902-5-336i

way a democratic parliament can operate is when the elected representatives of the people are able to express themselves as they see fit.
Those are the remarks I wanted to make, Mr. Chairman. However, I shall urge the government carefully to consider the points I raised. First of all, the dairy industry in eastern Canada; then, the prices paid for feed grain by eastern farmers in Canada; third, farm credit, and, more particularly the appointment of a vice president of the Farm Credit Corporation, and the possibility of increasing the loan ceiling so that family corporations may avail themselves of a higher loan limit than the present one of $20,000 or even $27,500; in the fourth instance the Three Rivers bridge. I would like the government to assume its responsibilities in that respect; in the fifth place I mentioned the $500 bonus. And finally I also dealt with federal-provincial relations.
Mr. Chairman, having said this, I shall conclude my remarks by asking this government to consider those six points in view of bringing about considerable improvement in those fields.

Mr. Chairman, before embarking on the main part of my remarks I want to refer for a moment to the figures which the leader of the N.D.P., the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, put on the record this afternoon. He was speaking about the Liberal promises and was recalling them from memory. I think it was a fairly accurate recollection, but since there has been a complete disregard of the promises which the Liberal party made in the last election campaign with respect to equalization payments I should like to put on the record what the promises were. I am reading from a pamphlet printed by the National Liberal Federation, 251 Cooper Street, Ottawa, entitled: "The Policies of the Liberal Party, General Election, 1963". On page 7 of that pamphlet we find these words under the heading "Equal Partners in Confederation":
Work well with the provinces. National unity and good government in Canada depend on cooperation between Ottawa and the provinces. The essential foundation for effective co-operation, in all matters of national concern, is full respect for the rights of the provinces in matters within their jurisdiction. All Liberal policies will be carried out with this full respect.
Provide full equalization of provincial revenues from the tax fields that the provinces share with the federal government.
This is the only way the provinces can afford similar standards of services, and so provide equality of opportunities for all Canadians. A new Liberal government will make equalization payments which bring the other provinces up to the level of the richest, in revenue per head from shared taxes.

This promise is just one of those several promises which have fallen by the wayside, which were expedient for the Liberal party to make during the election campaign, but which, when it comes to facing the hard facts of reality, and after speaking with the provincial premiers, they have discarded completely.
I asked earlier in the session why there was not some representation for the two northern territories in this federal-provincial conference. It might interest hon. members of the committee to know that the territorial governments signed five-year fiscal agreements which are exactly similar in all respects to the fiscal agreements signed by the federal government with the provinces.
As far as the territorial council of the Yukon is concerned, it is wholly elected and if it does not approve that fiscal arrangement it is not bound to sign it. It has full legislative authority in this regard. A similar situation exists in the Northwest Territories. I asked the acting prime minister yesterday, or the day before, what representation was given to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories at the dominion-provincial conference. He said, as has been said in the past, that the matter was being considered. There is a committee in the Yukon, consisting of three members of the council, which calls itself the advisory committee on finance. The commissioner of the territory, who is a federal civil servant, is required to sit with that committee during the process of preparing the territorial budget. The committee visits Ottawa once a year for the purpose of discussing with federal officials the fiscal affairs of the territory. The federal-provincial conference has made decisions with respect to indian affairs, public works, health and welfare and virtually every federal activity in the provinces and in the territory. I have not heard one member mention today the fact that there are Canadians who live in the north and who contribute to the revenue of this country. It seems to me that in this situation some voice should be heard from the territories before any new tax arrangements are entered into between the federal government and the provinces.
Perhaps through lack of information, perhaps through ignorance of the territories involved, members of this house and of the committee are prone to forget that 40 per cent of Canada's land mass lies north of the 60th parallel and that this is a region from which the federal government derives a substantial revenue. The Yukon, alone, provides 90 per cent of Canada's gold. It is true that much of this revenue finds its way back to the territory by way of provision for the construction of roads, the building of homes

for Indians and other federal projects. The fact remains that the territory government is autonomous. It has these democratic institutions set up and has virtually the same legislative powers as the provinces with certain exceptions. One of these lies in the field of natural resources, from which the federal government derives most of its revenue. This is why the federal government has the responsibility and duty to spend money in the north to encourage the development of resources which it owns on behalf of all Canadians. It is no excuse to say that, because the territory comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to at least some extent, it should not be represented at fiscal conferences such as that which has gone on in Ottawa this week. Since the federal government does own these resources it should speak in that capacity in these arrangements with the provinces; and that, I imagine, is what the minister has been doing at this conference. What I am concerned about is that no territorial voice has been heard at the conference to express the northern point of view.
The territorial council in the Yukon unanimously passed a resolution requesting representation at these federal-provincial discussions. I think that was a reasonable request, and the government should have had no difficulty about accepting it. The council did not go as far as to say there should be full representation at the conference. They wanted simply to sit in as observers, so that they could take back their observations to assist them in their deliberations in the territory. This session the council passed a resolution calling for expert assistance from the Department of Labour in connection with matters which were of concern to them in the Yukon. They also passed a resolution calling for assistance from the Department of Transport. The council has repeatedly passed resolutions asking for the extension of the emergency landing strip construction program in the Yukon. They say in their sessional proceedings that the reason continually given by the Department of Transport for not improving these facilities is the cost which would be involved. Surely this could be the subject matter for discussion at a conference of the kind which has been going on this week; it is a subject with which the council is properly concerned.
I express concern about the amount of expenditure of a federal nature which has gone into the northern territories in the past six years, and what is likely to be in the books for the future. I think many Canadians lose sight of the fact that the resources of the

Yukon and of the Northwest Territories belong to all Canadians. This parliament, because it has direct jurisdiction over the natural resources of these areas, has a responsibility and a duty to spend money for the purpose of developing these northern territories. If this approach is not made, these areas will remain undeveloped in direct proportion to the extent to which the federal government is disinterested in the development of the territory.
Upon returning to the house, after a visit I had made to the Yukon, I read with interest what had been said by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, when introducing his estimates. He indicated that the federal government would in future place much more reliance on private investment for the development of the territories than on a continuing program of development construction. I think this would be a tragic mistake. If the government does not continue the development road program which we instituted in the northern territories, together with the roads to resources program in the northern parts of the provinces, the effect will be to diminish private investment by corporations and others in the north. I obtained from the Minister of Transport an assurance that a new terminal building will be constructed in Whitehorse. This is a good thing. Of course, the decision was made by the previous government, though in a different form. The previous plan was to convert one of the existing hangars in the city. The minister has informed me that the new plan is to construct a new building.
The cost of conversion was too high.

I understand the reason why it was too high was because of the requirements, or demands of the Department of National Revenue and its customs and excise branch, as always seems to be the case when that particular department is concerned with public buildings. At any rate, the idea to give us a building is an extremely good one. We were all hoping it could have been constructed during the winter, in order to relieve the unemployment situation in the Yukon.
This is another area in which I think a word or two might be said. We heard all sorts of high flown promises during the last election campaign that unemployment was one of those matters that was going to be cured immediately upon the Liberal government taking office. The 60 days of decision were going to accomplish wonders. In very short order there would be full employment; that is how it was described. There seems to have been some disagreement among certain members of the Liberal cabinet. The Minister
Interim Supply
of Finance, for instance, said that full employment was not possible and I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce said the same thing. However, the Prime Minister went across the country saying that this was not an impossible achievement at all and that it would be accomplished. There were statements made by the Secretary of State. Here is one that was reported in Summerside on March 26, 1963 and in Charlottetown on March 27, 1963 in which the Secretary of State said:
It is the Liberal policy to see that every able person willing to work will have the opportunity to earn a decent living.
That is what he said. Now, in co-operation with the minister of northern affairs several years ago, I developed a program for creating jobs for the Indian people around the Yukon. I am sure all hon. members will agree with me when I say that this is one sector of our population that, instead of having to rely on welfare handouts, deserves job opportunities being created in order that they may keep their self-respect. This program that was developed was a program of slashing timber for rights of way for the construction of new development roads in both territories, I may say.
Now, I received a copy of a letter for which I asked, from the assistant deputy minister of northern affairs, dated August 16, 1963. This is on the deputy minister's stationery and reads as follows:
Just before leaving Ottawa you inquired about clearing on the Watson lake-Ross river road in the winter of 1963-64.
The department intends to clear 24 miles between mile 120 and mile 144. As previously, the work will be supervised by the Indian affairs branch and it is expected that about 40,000 man hours of labour will be provided at $1.60 per hour, and that approximately 100 workmen will be required.
It is signed by Mr. Cunningham, assistant deputy minister. I was very happy when I received that letter because it meant that these jobs were going to be made available to people who sorely needed jobs. When I got back to Whitehorse I made an announcement which was published in the press, and the Liberal organization was quite annoyed that a Conservative member had access to this information which, after all, is public. In any event, I understand the minister raised quite a ruckus when he got back to his department, trying to find out who had passed this information on to me. The upshot of this whole thing has been that the program has been cancelled, I understand. I think the reason for its cancellation is simply an endeavour to embarrass me politically, and I feel that is a very sad state of affairs.
A decision was made by the government to go ahead with the slashing program. The

Interim Supply
announcement was made, and unfortunately it was not made by the minister when he visited the Yukon. As soon as he returned, I discovered that the program had been cancelled. What the minister is doing by cancelling the program is putting 100 men out of work and denying 40,000 man hours of labour to people in the Yukon who sorely need it. It seems to me that this particular project deserves some consideration.
I see the Minister of Transport in his seat and I should like to draw to his attention the proceedings during the last session of the Yukon council during which there was a request for the officials of his department to visit the Yukon for the purpose of sitting down with the council to discuss airport costs. There is the question of lengthening the runways at Mayo, or constructing a new airport there. The huge iron ore holdings of the companies north of Mayo demand that there should be some efficient transportation link set up for the purpose of encouraging that development. It would not need to be restricted to that area, but the whole central portion of the Yukon could be considered because there are potentially rich resources there and there should be an airport of higher standard than the one existing. The excuse the council is always getting from the minister's department is the high cost. They have asked for someone to discuss the problem with them.
I turn now to post offices. This business of employment is a very interesting one. Unemployment was the subject of a hue and cry by the Liberals while they were conducting the last two election campaigns, and it is the subject on which the least amount of effort has been exerted by them during the months they have been in office. Perhaps I am a little unfair there, because there has been some increase in employment, particularly amongst the ranks of the Liberal party and particularly in the Post Office Department. It seems that there has been a rash of appointments and a rash of discharged employees in the post offices across this country. It appears that the purpose of this move is to replace existing office holders who are not Liberal supporters with those who are.
I am very sorry to observe that the fair program of calling for tenders for every mail contract in the last six years in the Yukon has now been discarded. I understand these contracts are being allotted by appointment on the basis of selections made by the government. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with your consent, I will try to explain Bill S-46 in the shortest possible time.
Bill S-46 is an act to amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act. Its purpose is to amend

the 1954 act, which had itself been amended in 1957. The purpose of Bill S-46 is twofold:
1.	To make it easier for the two savings banks concerned to appoint directors;
2.	To authorize the two banks concerned to make loans on the security of first mortgages up to 60 per cent, instead of 40 per cent as is the case at the present time.
You will notice in clause 2 of Bill S-46 that the two banks concerned are:
1.	The Montreal City and District Savings Bank.
2.	The Quebec Savings Bank.
I believe that the explanatory notes on the bill are plain enough with respect to the results ensuing from the proposed amendments.
There are three clauses in the bill which I move tonight.
The first one is to vary the qualifications required from the directors. According to the present legislation, a director must hold $5,000 worth of stock; the purpose of this bill is to replace $5,000 by 500 shares.
The second clause of the bill is to reduce the value of the shares from $10 to $1 a share. Under the present legislation, a director must hold $5,000 worth of stock, that is 500 shares at $10 each. Now, the shares of the two banks in question sell at a price well above $10. As far as the Montreal City and District Savings Bank is concerned, they sell at $160 each, and as regards the Quebec Savings Bank, $74 each; so that according to the present legislation one must be the owner of $80,000 in shares to become a director of the Montreal savings bank and of $35,000 in shares to become a director of the Quebec Savings Bank.
I submit with respect to the members of the house, and to you, Mr. Chairman, that those amounts are too high. Those two banks have directors aged 70 and over. Those men must be replaced by younger directors and you cannot easily find a young man with ability and that kind of money.
So, the combined effect of those two clauses is to reduce those amounts to some $8,000 and $3,500 respectively.
The third clause of this bill is quite simple. Its purpose is to replace 40 per cent by 60 per cent.
In brief, the purpose of those three clauses is this: the first two clauses are to facilitate the election of new directors in the two banks, and the third clause is to authorize those two banks to lend up to 60 per cent of their deposit liabilities.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: BROADCASTING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-30, to amend the Broadcasting Act (community antenna).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill should really be read in connection with my companion Bill C-49, to amend the Radio Act. In the Broadcasting Act as it was enacted and assented to in December, 1958, section 10 gives these objects and purposes:
The board shall, for the purpose of ensuring the continued existence and efficient operation of a national broadcasting system and the provision of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service of a high standard that is basically Canadian in content and character, regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto.
I would like to turn to section 2(b) where "broadcasting" is defined as follows:
"broadcasting" means the dissemination of any form of radio electric communication, including radiotelegraph, radiotelephone, the wireless transmission of writing, signs, signals, pictures and sounds of all kinds by means of Hertzian waves, intended to be received by the public either directly or through the medium of relay stations;
I would point out that this amendment would change that definition so that "broadcasting" would have added to it:
The redissemination for commercial gain of broadcast matter by wired transmission intended to be received by private persons.
The reason for introducing this amendment is that I think the national purposes, the national objects of the Broadcasting Act are beginning to be affected more and more by the growth and development of the community antenna systems, or so-called wired systems. On April 17, 1963, the board of broadcast governors, who had referred to this problem a number of times in its annual report, including a reference on page 19 of its report for 1961-62, issued this press release:

Broadcasting Act
The board has for some months now been concerned with the effect of the distribution of television programs by means of cable systems on the distribution of programs by broadcasting stations. The board's concern centres around the fact that broadcasting stations, as a condition of licence, are directed by law to achieve certain national purposes. Distribution of programs by cable system is not so directed. Thus, if the achievement of national purposes is threatened by the use of cable systems, the board feels it should be in a position to draw attention to the conditions which create a threat and to recommend such action as it deems necessary to the preservation of the achievement of the national purposes.
In order to receive evidence, opinions, arguments and suggestions, the board will hold a public hearing on the general subject of the relationship between the development of wired television systems and broadcasting, and broadcasting policy.
The board seeks representations from broadcasters. An opportunity would be given to operators of wired systems to make representations, if they wish to do so. The board is hopeful that groups of citizens who are neither broadcasters nor operators of wired systems will contribute their opinions on the matters outlined in the notice of hearing.
Because of the vital nature of this hearing in the whole area of serving the national purposes through the broadcast media, the board is making arrangements to have the proceedings transmitted on both radio and television.
I do not even know whether the board had the power, but no one questioned their power. Anyway, they did call these hearings and I will refer to them later. I should like to point out that it has been the custom here for many years to have a special committee on broadcasting. In 1960-61 this committee met. I have in my hand a volume of the evidence-it is very thick-and amongst the evidence heard were representations with regard to wired systems. In the final report of this special committee one of the recommendations made was No. 4, which appears at page 992:
That the governor in council consider the expediency of making reference to the Supreme Court of Canada for the purpose of determining:
(i)	the constitutional jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada as to those means of electronic communication known as wired systems;
(ii)	and, in the affirmative, whether such wired systems are covered by the word "broadcasting" as presently defined under paragraph (b) of section 2 of the Broadcasting Act, 1958.
At those same hearings there was a report of the committee on wired systems. I may not be completely accurate here, because I have not been able to track it down as yet in the hearings, but as I understand it the members of this committee included the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, the Department of Transport, the members of the board of broadcast governors and members of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. They presented this fairly substantial report which had a number of conclusions, and I would like to put the conclusions on the record. I wish to do so because I think it is necessary at this time, in suggesting this

amendment, that the house should know I am not trying to cut the throats of the community antenna people in any way, shape or form. They perform a very real and important function in many parts of the country. I want to come at it from the point of view of the preceding history and the fact that things are changing very rapidly and we need to do something about it. It seems to me that we need to do something about it in terms of the framework of the national purposes which have been the objective of the broadcasting system in Canada since it was developed early in the 1930's-I might point out, by a Conservative government-and have been carried on and confirmed ever since by succeeding governments, royal commissions and committees of the house. These were the conclusions of this special committee on wired systems:
The evidence of the growth of television broadcasting since 1952, the substantial coverage already achieved, and the emergence of "second" television stations suggests that the policies and regulations designed to advance the national purposes have not been seriously inhibiting in their effects. The comparatively small total coverage of wired systems suggests that the service offered by them has not had a significant retarding effect on television broadcasting generally.
This was in 1961:
In some situations community antenna television systems have provided service where television service was not otherwise possible. To the extent that these systems have extended the coverage of Canadian television broadcast services, they have made a positive contribution to the national purpose; and are continuing to do so.
I might say amen to that:
In other situations where they compete with local television broadcasting, they provide alternative viewing by extension of Canadian and U.S. signals. The extension of the reception of U.S. signals does nothing to advance the national purposes. However, the general effect does not appear to have been significantly detrimental to the national purposes. The operations of some broadcasting stations affiliated with the corporation may be less profitable than in the absence of competition from wired systems; and some reduction in the costs of the national public serveie might result from the elimination of the wired system. It might also be easier for the board of broadcast governors to apply its regulations. But it does not seem that these factors are so substantial as to justify a general extension of controls over wired systems, having in mind that regulations similar to those now applying to television broadcasting would prevent any CATV system from carrying signals of U.S. stations. However, in marginal situations, it must be conceded that the introduction or increase in the service of wired systems could prejudice the national purposes required of broadcasting.
My point here is that in 1961 the effect was not considered inhibiting, but it was pointed out that the introduction or increase in the service of wired systems could prejudice the national purposes required of broadcasting. The submission goes on:

It has been pointed out earlier that there is no doubt that some aspects of the operation of CATV systems could be brought under the terms of the Broadcasting Act. (There is some doubt as to whether all aspects of CATV operations could be included). It has also been pointed out that CATV systems are licensed by the Department of Transport.
That is all I wanted to read from this point of view, except the final sentence, which is:
Because of the board's responsibility-
That is, the board of broadcast governors:
-for the national objectives under the Broadcasting Act, and the similarity between the end results (television reception) of television broadcasting and the closed circuit system, the board of broadcast governors should be expected to keep informed on the development of closed circuit systems, and if necessary to report to the minister on their impact on television broadcasting.
This particular committee report also has an appendix A which sets out the commercial broadcasting and receiving stations, the community antenna television systems and the rules and regulations under which they operate. It is my contention that the situation has now been reached where the size of the community antenna television audience is large enough that we need to consider its impact on the national purpose. It is my contention that we should bring it under the definition of broadcasting in the act so we can be sure that in its future extension it does not cripple the present licence holders and the objectives of the national system.
I should like to point out that I specifically say "commercial" in the bill, because there are a great many community antenna television set-ups in Canada that are formed on a co-operative basis or on a non-profit basis, particularly in smaller towns, or they may be provided by companies in company towns to many of the residents of those towns. My specific purpose is to bring under the act the mushrooming development of very strong, powerful, commercial organizations that are beginning to establish community antenna systems very widely, which are promoted well and in such a way that they are getting the kind of response that is digging very strongly into what I conceive to be the national purpose and the effectiveness of the present licence holders of radio and television stations.
I might refer to the promotional material of Lakehead Videon which operates in my own area. They have gone from a very small number of subscribers until they are up in the thousands now. They do a very good job of pushing their service. I have a kind of brochure of theirs here which sets out how cable television works and points out that subscribers can get three extra American channels as a result of their service. They also offer a certain number of specials, such as 28902-5-337
Broadcasting Act
fights and other sporting events that are available on their service which, as far as I am concerned, extend them beyond just the normal area and turn them into real competitors of the broadcasting stations. I want to make it very clear that the response to Lake-head Videon in my own area is such that it would be very unpopular if any regulation led to the cancelling of the kind of service they are providing. I would be persona non grata. I want to emphasize again that this is not my intention.
I have a Canadian Press report of the meeting of the board of broadcast governors last June which I should like to put on the record, because it is the best summary I have been able to find and encompasses what took place at their meeting. It is found in the Gazette of June 5, 1963 and reads as follows:
Public and private broadcasters sided together Tuesday before the board of broadcast governors in expressing fears of a potential threat to their existence in the event of the development of closed circuit pay T.V. on a national scale.
"They're five feet high and risin'," said R. C. Fraser, C.B.C. vice president for corporate affairs, of the recent growth of community antenna (cable) systems in Canada.
Added Spencer Caldwell, president of the rival privately owned C.T.V. Television Network Limited: "There is a possibility that if cable T.V. reached such proportions that it reduced our revenues and ratings, it would make it difficult for us to achieve our national purpose as broadcasters."
In reply, F. T. Metcalfe of Guelph, Ont., president of the national community antenna television association, said: "Basically, the real threat to a national purpose in broadcasting is that the Canadian viewer wants a choice of service".
He contended that in effect, most of Canada's 322 community antenna systems serving some 200,000 households are only a superior aerial service, making possible improved reception of Canadian and U.S. signals. They were not in competition with broadcasters.
The public session was called by the B.B.G. to give persons associated with the broadcasting industry an opportunity to air opinions about the relationship of wired systems with licensed television stations.
B.B.G. vice chairman Carlyle Allison said the broadcasting industry's concern is with the future extension of wired systems to "the possible detriment of what is called 'free television'." The B.B.G. did not intend to make a recommendation to the transport minister following the hearing, he said, but would provide a summary of opinions expressed so the government itself could determine whether any further actions is required.
The broadcasters differed in their specific recommendations but all were agreed in essence that the possible linkage of community antenna systems into what in effect would be a closed circuit national network would pose a serious threat to them.
I will not go on with the points that were made. It seems to me that is a fairly good summary. I should like to refer to some missionary work that was done by the president of the national community antenna television association of Canada, Mr. Metcalfe. I have been in touch with him, have been

Broadcasting Act
interviewed by him and have had a number of letters from him. One of the points he made to me was that I was carrying a torch for the private broadcasters and he thought this was a most retrograde step for a person identified with my particular party. I want to make it perfectly clear I do not feel like carrying a torch for the private broadcasters, except in the sense that if we in parliament set up a licensing and regulating authority, force some persons to operate under it and then by not acting allow some other kind of agency operating in the same field to come in and undercut the persons we have charged a licence fee and whom we require to do certain things, I think we have a responsibility to look at the situation and see whether it is on all fours with simple equity. It is in this sense that I have brought forward the bill.

speechtext:
This is brought up in a number of places in the literature I have, and I am not going to go into it because as far as I am concerned it is a morass. For example, as I understand the situation the Telemeter subscription system in Etobicoke would not be affected by this particular change in the act. My point is that what would be brought under the act by my amendment would be any system operated for a profit that took out of the air Hertzian waves and rebroadcast them to wired sets in homes. That is as far as I want to go with respect to the point the hon. gentleman raised. There are some differences of opinion, and perhaps the minister who speaks for the government in this regard may be able to clear them up.
Finally, in relation to Mr. Metcalfe and the national community antenna television association, I want to say that they made a very good case in the brief they presented to the board of broadcast governors that they should not be put under the act and under the control of that board. Personally I do not feel their case is good enough. I think that the extension, particularly in terms of the skill and the capital they have behind them, is such that the thing is really going to become sweeping. I know, for example, that the owner of the Montreal Alouettes, Mr. Workman, intends to get into this field-I believe he is already in it in order to push his football games and other sporting events. I

know that at the present time there is a setup in Toronto for the rebroadcasting of certain hockey games which may be extended. I feel that this bill would not apply to the telecasting of Montreal Alouette games by means of a wired system, as long as the actual picture presented is not taken off something which is sent out by means of the so-called Hertzian waves. I know from contacts I have had that the wired systems are growing in number very quickly. It is only logical to assume that in the very near future they will be in a position to provide what is in effect a network. I am not concerned, and I do not think other members should be, over the kind of financial set-up they may have or how they extend their system. But when you have in effect a system which is competing in the same kind of programming with the licensed stations and with our national corporation, it seems to me it is time we acted.
It was more in the spirit of encouraging the government to accept what I think is their responsibility than with any intent to create havoc among the community antenna people that I brought forward this bill and a sister or brother bill to amend the Radio Act. If the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) would care to make a comment from the point of view of the attitude of the government on this question, I am sure not only I but everyone in broadcasting would be very interested in his remarks.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BROADCASTING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much time in what is an hour which I think should be properly devoted to members of the house who do not sit on the treasury benches, but the hon. gentleman has invited me to express a view and I feel that this is a matter of very grave national importance.
In the 1920's when radio broadcasting began to grow in this country it was the view of the government of that day, a view shared in the early thirties by the Conservative government which succeeded the government in office in the twenties, that radio broadcasting could have such an important influence upon our country that it was a matter of major concern to Canada, our being, as we were then and still are, a country with a population about one tenth that of the country to the south of us. The governments of those days felt it was important that radio broadcasting should therefore be Canadian.
I do not think that importance has diminished one whit with the years. We have taken the view about private corporations that broadcast as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has indicated, that they must be licensed by the public authority. We have also taken the view that they must be owned

predominantly by Canadians, and I think that that is the right view to take. I do not think that anyone in this house of any party would seriously argue that there should be allowed to take place any development that it is within the power of this parliament to control or to legislate about, which would indirectly undermine what has over a period of 40 years- indeed, ever since the beginning of broadcasting, or licensed broadcasting, assumed any real importance in our community life-been regarded as a matter of national importance, a matter perhaps affecting the very existence of our country as a separate entity. With television, of course, I think the influence is far more pervasive.
This community antenna system has many things to commend it. I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Port Arthur that a community antenna system which merely provides better reception for broadcasting in any given area is highly to be commended, and perhaps it is the only way that many communities in this country which are somewhat remote and isolated, particularly in constituencies like those represented by the hon. member himself and by me, can expect to get good reception.
But it is quite another matter if a system is to be created which can do indirectly what we do not permit broadcasters themselves to do directly. If community antennae are to be put up in places like Winnipeg and Vancouver for the purpose of bringing in United States stations which would not be allowed to broadcast in Canada, then it seems to me it is perfectly clear that the intent of parliament, which I believe must have influenced every successive government which believed in the view that it is the intent of the Canadian people, is thereby being circumvented.
In the few months I have been a minister I have taken a very serious view of this problem, as has my colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) as well. At the present moment, or almost at the present moment because this morning I read one of the papers on the subject in the few minutes I had before coming into the house, we are giving very careful consideration to recommendations which we feel we ought to bring before our colleagues as to possible courses of action in this field. I have not, and neither has the Minister of Transport, had the time or the opportunity yet to discuss this matter with my colleagues. Therefore I am not attempting, and it would be wrong for me to attempt, to indicate what disposition the government feels it should make of this matter or what disposition it feels it should ask parliament to make.
28902-5-337J
Broadcasting Act
I have the impression-this is one reason the hon. gentleman has, of course, introduced the bill-that there must be some amendment to the law, if there is to be any kind of effective control of competition of a kind which would not be permitted by broadcasters themselves, Canadian broadcasters, in this field. It seems to me that it is very likely that there will have to be legislation of that sort; but precisely what form it ought to take, how far it should go, and so on, is something which it would be very presumptuous of me, with the rather scanty information I have on the subject, to attempt to say at this stage. However, I have no hesitation in saying that the position of this government, and I hope it is the position of the whole house, is perfectly clear-that we intend to do everything we can to see that broadcasting remains substantially, to the greatest degree we can reasonably make it, Canadian.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, along with the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) I have been a member of the broadcasting committee, and I think this was one of those points on which the hon. gentleman and I were in accord without too much difficulty during the hearings of that committee. Over the past years I had a considerable amount to do with broadcasting, in my position of parliamentary secretary to the minister of national revenue; and this matter was one which exercised me a good deal.
It has been suggested that the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act were not sufficiently broad in their wording to include what is really known as broadcasting by wired systems. With all due respect to the hon. gentlemen who held that view, I felt there was a very strong argument that the act as presently designated covers the subject matter. It will be remembered that the question of federal jurisdiction over broadcasting was referred to the supreme court many years ago and the reference at that time included dissemination by means of Hertzian waves. If we look at the act itself, at section 2(b) we find a definition of broadcasting given. Since "broadcasting" includes the dissemination of any form of radio electric communication intended to be received by the public either directly or through the medium of relay stations, I think there is a highly arguable case for the contention I am now putting forward. In line 2 of paragraph (a) of clause 2 of the bill, after the words "radio electric communication" the text goes on to say: "including-" -that does not mean including exclusively; it means "including"-"radio telegraph, radio telephone, the wireless transmission of writing, signs, signals, pictures and sounds of all kinds by means of Hertzian waves intended

Broadcasting Act
to be received-", and so on. Notwithstanding a good deal of argument to the contrary, I have not been persuaded that my interpretation of the act in this regard is entirely wrong.

subtopic: BROADCASTING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he not agree that up to the present time both the broadcasting industry and the sponsors of community antennae have taken the attitude that the definition does not cover these systems?

subtopic: BROADCASTING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
In that regard, I know the advice given to various bodies has raised some doubt about whether they are covered. Without telling tales out of school I think it would be fair to say that the board of broadcast governors, who are concerned about this matter, felt it might be unwise for them to embark upon a program of controlling this form of broadcasting activity only to find, perhaps after having been taken to court, that they had no authority to do so. I suggest it is for that reason they have not acted. This is a lawyer's law. As long as it does not hurt anyone too much, it is difficult to get an amendment passed.
If this proposal were to be acted upon now, I would be in favour of it. I am fully in favour of what the hon. member has proposed, and I think the Secretary of State, too, is ad idem with the hon. member. It has been the purpose of the Broadcasting Act and of all parliaments since the 'thirties, emphasized and underlined by successive royal commissions and governments, both Liberal and Conservative, that there should be no division in this regard and that broadcasting is to be the subject of a definite aim. We have a national broadcasting policy outlined in the Broadcasting Act which prescribes the duties of the board of broadcast governors on the one hand and of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the other. As to the proposition put forward with regard to these isolated areas, these community areas where the system proposed would ensure a clear signal to those with television sets, that is all right. But even now-and I could cite cases- applications to build a reception tower with a microwave relay to another tower for dissemination thereafter by cable must be submitted under the Radio Act to the Minister of Transport, and there is an informal reference to the board of broadcast governors. There is already partial control but it is not as overt as it should be.
What is the danger about informal broadcasting? It is, really, what I consider to be the possibility of creating glorified satellites of United States stations along the southern border of our country. We have set up regulations which govern the operation of our

Canadian systems. These look to the financial stability of applicants. Licences are withheld or deferred on the basis of economic considerations. Yet if it is permitted to establish without restraint wire systems which are, in effect, satellites of non-Canadian stations we would be defeating the whole purpose of our broadcasting policy. I know there are some of these so-called wire systems which are really baby stations. At certain periods during the day they introduce news broadcasts and sports broadcasts into their program schedules. Where does one stop? One might then introduce local programs.

subtopic: BROADCASTING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext: And commercials.

subtopic: BROADCASTING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member for Port Arthur says you begin to slip in the odd commercial. This is natural and you would then have a baby station operating without any control.
I, myself, think such stations must be brought under supervision of the board of broadcast governors. I would have hoped to see this done earlier, because millions of dollars have already been invested in this direction and if action is deferred too long the situation becomes set, economically. Suppose legislation is then introduced to bring these wire systems under the control of the board of broadcast governors. There may be good reason why some of them should be eliminated; yet this could not be done because to take action would be to operate to the detriment of a business established quite legally under the law as it existed.
However, as I say, my view is that the board of broadcast governors already has power in this regard under the interpretation I have placed upon the act. Perhaps the quickest way to solve this difficulty would be for the board to act on one of these cases -to have one of these companies summoned to court to show cause. This might be quicker than trying to get the government to amend the act. I do not know. But with the purpose or objective of this bill I am in full accord, though I hope action can be taken without the formality of making an amendment at this stage.

subtopic: BROADCASTING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING CONTROL OVER COMMUNITY ANTENNA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) that, personally, I do not share at all his opinion with regard to his proposed object in introducing this bill.
Those sections which complement Bill C-49 are very short; indeed, it is not a question of changing the definition of the term "broadcasting", but only of giving it a broader sense. However, I believe that this bill could seriously affect a very great number of T.V. viewers.

This proposed amendment of the Broadcasting Act and Radio Act will result in placing T.V. community aerials systems or other similar operations under the control and supervision of the board of broadcast governors, if I understand the explanatory notes accompanying the bills.
Personally, I feel that the board has enough authority as it is, and that it should not be allowed to interfere in a field which is not its concern, especially in view of the nature of this system and of the service it renders.
In addition, I truly fear for the freedom of viewers who can now select the program or channel of their choice. Indeed, under Department of Transport regulations, licenses are issued only for systems which meet the technical and mechanical requirements concerning, for instance, the height and location of antennas, the type of cable used, the territory served, and the signals which are received and transmitted.
Mr. Speaker, I also feel that the result of those regulations is to restrict the broadcasting of television programs by cable to the waves that can already be received in a given area through proper equipment or antenna.
It is essential, of course, that regulations should be applied to ensure the orderly and proper operation of this system.
In order to be in a position to decide whether it is advisable or necessary to pass this legislation, it would be necessary to know something about the services rendered by this system and the part it plays in the broadcasting of programs.
At present, television signals are picked up by two mediums in areas more or less distant from broadcasting stations; first of all, through the adjunction of one or several individual antennas, which is the first and only method possible in many areas. Generally, this method is rather costly for the owners of television sets. In addition, it involves a great deal of inconvenience, without ensuring an adequate reception in spite of the high standard of the receiving set or of the broadcasting stations.
On the other hand, a group of individuals or a corporation may set up at a location that lends itself to the reception of waves, a tower or powerful community antenna that would surely be more costly, but the cost of which could be divided among all users. They would thus be assured of a much better reception from distant or low-power stations, as well as of a wider variety of programs.
In short, this is only an extension of the usual antenna, except that a main antenna is located in a place where reception is better and where interference is reduced to a minimum.
Broadcasting Act
This antenna, as any another ordinary antenna, can only pick up signals which can already reach a given area. It neither reduces nor adds anything to the broadcast, it does not alter in any way the waves which are merely picked up and retransmitted. It is an absolutely passive element which moreover does not interfere in the public field.
It can be claimed, that in such a case, the need has created the means.
Some ten years ago, there were few, if any, such organizations in this country.
Today, there are more than 300, with an average of 800 subscribers for every system. A total of 240,000 homes, that is about a million people, are served by such systems.
And more than half of those systems operate in the province of Quebec.
I remember that about ten years ago, more particularly in the eastern townships, we had to set up expensive individual antennas, which frequently did not work because of storm damage, on account of the distance from Montreal, for topographical reasons or due to the mountains around us. In fact, we were getting better pictures from stations on the other side of the border, in the United States, and I think that this was the case of all areas near the American border.
Now, thanks to that system, we are able to watch Canadian stations, and more particularly those of Montreal, which was formerly impossible.
And we now have a choice between two fine relay systems, and can enjoy television of a quality we never knew before.
Those systems are appreciated by all their users. They supply us with very high-grade television at a very reasonable rate and they enable us to watch Canadian programs in our district, which are generally excellent, even if there is room for improvement.
The subscribers have a diversified choice and are completely free to watch whatever program they like.
The local broadcasting stations have no reason to fear such a system, for it multiplies the number of telespectators and thus increases the audience which can enjoy its favourite programs.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that any additional regulations would be unnecessary and unwelcome. It might interfere with the liberty of the individual, who wants to be able to choose whatever program he pleases.
Mr. Speaker, I see that it is six o'clock. I had several things to add. I hope that I will be able to continue my remarks if and when Bill C-49 comes before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the last time the estimates of the Department of Industry were under consideration it was suggested that a statement would be made by the Minister of Industry on the various activities with which he was charged, covering all of them; that this might well be followed by general statements by hon. members on all of these activities; and this would be followed by a detailed examination of the estimates of each of the several departments in the order I indicated.
The order I suggested was first the Department of Industry, then atomic energy, then the Department of Defence Production, the national research council and finally the department of public printing and stationery. I have made some remarks regarding the Department of Industry and regarding atomic energy, and this evening I will speak on the activities of the Department of Defence Production, the department of public printing and stationery, and finally the national research council.
Under the provisions of the Defence Production Act the Minister of Defence Production has exclusive authority to buy or otherwise acquire the defence supplies required by the Department of National Defence. Although the Department of Defence Production was itself established in 1951, the government's policy under which defence procurement is undertaken by a separate civilian agency dates back to the early days of world
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten).]
war II. As I pointed out to the special committee on defence on July 30, at that time-[DOT]
-the Canadian government decided the procurement ot goods and services required for defence purposes would be under the control of a separate civilian organization staffed by people who, through experience, had become experts in the purchasing field. This permits the Department of National Defence to concentrate on military functions and, through unified buying procedures, tends to reduce the costs and bring the taxpayer the best possible value for the dollars that are spent on defence material.
This responsibility for the procurement of defence supplies is of very great importance. However, there are other additional responsibilities which are of almost equal significance. My department has the responsibility for defence development and production sharing with the United States, defence export activities with other friendly countries, and the co-ordination of Canadian activities in connection with the research, development and production program of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
In addition the government has adopted certain recommendations of the royal commission on government organization in respect to the establishment of a central purchasing agency to serve all departments and agencies, both civil and military, of the federal government, other than commercially oriented crown corporations, and also in respect to the transfer of certain responsibilities of the department of public printing and stationery. These decisions are of great importance to the Department of Defence Production, and I shall deal with these matters in greater detail later on.
As will be seen from the estimates which have been tabled, the most significant increase over the 1962-63 estimates is found under vote 25 covering development sharing. The purpose of vote 25 is to sustain technological capability in Canadian defence industry by supporting selected defence development programs. This has stimulated development activity to a marked degree. It has resulted too in other benefits such as maintaining capabilities and putting the companies in a position to obtain work in related fields. Initial sales of doppler navigation equipment, sonobuoys, Caribou STOL aircraft and turbo aircraft engines, for example, indicate yield ratios of 10 to one in dollars spent for development to export sales received. One project, which was assisted financially to the extent of approximately $1 million, has accomplished $30 million in defence sales.
Another item which I have mentioned is the Canada-U.S. defence production sharing program. This has resulted in 4J years of useful activity in Canadian industry. This

program, in essence, aims at optimum mutual utilization of the Canadian and U.S. defence industrial capability. Arrangements include providing equal opportunity for Canadian industry to participate with U.S. industry on the competitive bases of price, delivery and technical competence to meet North American defence requirements.
Sustained effort in the past four years by both governments and their defence industries has resulted in such major achievements as the exemption of certain Canadian defence material under the provisions of the buy American act, the duty free entry of such material into the United States, and increasing response of Canadian industry to United States defence procurement opportunities. Defence development and production sharing ramifications have become widespread throughout Canadian industry, and a large proportion of Canadian research and development capability is oriented towards United States and mutual defence requirements.
In terms of Canadian industrial activity generated by the program, the total of United States defence production sharing business placed with Canadian companies in the 4| years to the end of June 1963, amounted to about $657 million. For the last full calendar year, 1962, this business totalled about $254 million. This was a 75 per cent increase over 1961, due largely to contracts for Caribou aircraft and a contribution by the United States to the joint Canada-U.S. F104G aircraft program. On the other hand, Canadian defence production sharing business in the United States amounted to some $127 million in 1962. The total for the 4J years of the program is about $574 million. While the balance of production sharing business between Canada and the United States had been some $47 million in favour of the United States at the beginning of 1962, it had at least temporarily reversed by the end of June, 1963, to about $83 million in Canada's favour. This achievement of mutually advantageous reciprocal procurement I consider to be very worth while indeed. Over 300 Canadian companies have received contracts since this program began, and the achievements of some of these companies is a clear indication that participation in the United States defence market is of outstanding benefit. I feel that Canadian industry deserves great credit for its efforts in this regard.
Both the Canadian and United States governments have recognized that Canada's ability to participate in future defence industrial production programs would be lost without continuing research and development projects in Canada, and the future role of Canadian defence industry would therefore be confined to the production of the more
Supply-Industry
simple items of hardware. As a consequence, our ability to contribute to equipment programs for the defence of North America would be seriously weakened. Since 1959 substantial sums have been provided to assist Canadian companies to undertake development projects for both United States and other allied programs. As a result, a significant amount of research and development work has been stimulated in Canadian industry. Since 1959 to the end of August, 1963, a total of some 130 development sharing projects valued at about $76 million have been initiated in Canadian industry with funding support from the government, Canadian industry and other governments. Of this total, Canadian government support from vote 25 amounts to $32 million. Clearly there is now a greatly increased awareness in Canadian industry of the need to undertake research and development activities. To further reinforce this development sharing activity the United States secretary of defence and I have this month signed a memorandum of understanding in the field of co-operative development between our two departments.
My department's efforts in the development field are co-ordinated with the defence industrial research program which was initiated in 1961 by the defence research board. This program represents another step forward in our efforts to maintain Canadian scientific skills, and to ensure that the results of government defence research are made available to Canadian industry so that our industry can participate more effectively in the development and supply of defence equipments needed by the United States and other allies.
In concluding my remarks on production and development sharing, I want to emphasize the importance that is attached to this program of co-operation by ourselves and by the United States government. I refer to my report to the house on June 7, following my meeting with the United States secretary of defence, when I said in part:
Our meeting was held in a spirit of great cordiality and reaffirmed positively the intention of both our countries to continue to support a defence production sharing program. Assurances were given that the difficulties experienced by both countries in respect of balance of payments problems should not be allowed to interfere with the continuation and enlargement of this program-
The maintenance of a general balance of our reciprocal cross-border procurement of equipment seems the best answer to concern at the drain on foreign exchange reserves through such procurement.
For the future, as in the past, Canada expects to procure from United States defence industry those items which it does not make economic sense to try to produce in Canada. In return we look to continuing opportunities for Canadian industry to supply United States defence requirements where Canadian companies can compete on the basis of price, quality and delivery.
