speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
It was not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to cover those particular topics in these general remarks; but if there is interest in them, I will be very glad to report later on. I should now like to review the departmental role in the NATO program of co-operation in research, development and production and in the field of overseas defence export activity generally.
Unilateral weapon development is gradually becoming a thing of the past in most countries and this trend has a particular and critical significance for Canada. Our defence industrial planning must, therefore, to an increasing degree take into consideration foreign as well as Canadian military requirements and must be harmonized with defence development and production plans of NATO and other allied countries. Today, more than ever before, national efforts to participate in defence production programs of other countries are being intensified and international collaboration in defence research, development and production is possible only where appropriate government to government arrangements are established within which sales activity on the part of industry can achieve positive results. The primary role for government in this field is, therefore, development of bilateral, trilateral or multilateral arrangements based on specific areas of national technical capability which can be utilized to meet common requirements.
In planning the current re-organization of the department, careful attention has been given to the establishment of a management group which can provide effective central direction of our over-all department defence export activities as they relate to United States and other NATO and allied countries. While the Canadian Commercial Corporation has played a valuable part in these departmental activities, its function has been gradually assumed over the years by the Department of Defence Production. Complete integration of the working staff of this crown corporation into the department has now become essential. Accordingly, arrangements are in hand toward implementation of the recommendation of the royal commission on government, organization that management

and staff for activities of the corporation be provided by the Department of Defence Production.
A new international programs branch is being established to consolidate these activities of the Canadian Commercial Corporation with the staff co-ordination work of our United States and overseas divisions and thus to provide effective guidance and control of all of these elements of our departmental defence export activities within a single branch.
My department is responsible for co-ordination of Canadian activities within the NATO program of co-operation in defence research, development and production and provides the Canadian representative on the NATO armaments committee which administers the program. Arrangements are now in hand for strengthening this representation.
Canada has submitted for consideration by NATO groups a number of projects in the aircraft, armament and electronics fields. Canadian aircraft and electronics firms have submitted design proposals in response to specific NATO requests. There has been a broadening of the exchange of information on national research, development and production programs. As a concrete result of our active participation in the NATO armaments committee, and on the invitation of Canada and the United States, four other NATO countries are participating in a cooperative research and development program on a counter mortar radar being developed by a Canadian firm. A Canadian-Norwegian plan for joint production of our combined requirements of the M72 light anti-tank rocket has been approved as a NATO program. Other NATO countries have been invited to consider participation in the Canada-United Kingdom joint development of a short range surveillance system using an unmanned aerial vehicle known as the CL-89.
May I restate the responsibilities of the Minister of Defence Production as being, first, to procure the goods and services required by the Department of National Defence and, second, to ensure that the necessary production capacity is available in Canada to support our defence production program. These responsibilities form the basis for our over-all departmental defence export activities which include the defence development and production sharing program with the United States, armament co-operation within NATO, and bilateral defence production arrangements with NATO and other allied countries.
The increasing tendency toward complexity and high cost in weapon development and production make it essential that every avenue of co-operation with our allies be explored

in efforts to make the most effective use of our respective national resources in terms of funds, manpower and technological capabilities. At the same time we cannot overlook the benefit to the Canadian economy of performance in Canada to the greatest extent possible of the research, development and production associated with advanced weapon technology.
There are two additional matters which already have been of great importance to the Department of Defence Production and which will no doubt be of even greater significance in the future. These are, first, the recommendations of the royal commission on government organization and, second, the establishment of the new Department of Industry.
The royal commission on government organization, better known as the Glassco commission, included in its report the following recommendations, in addition to that already mentioned in respect of the Canadian Commercial Corporation:
That a central purchasing agency be established to serve all departments and agencies, both civil and military, of the federal government other than commercially oriented crown corporations.
That the Department of Defence Production be renamed the department of purchasing and supply and its responsibility be extended to include procurement for civilian departments and agencies.
That the new department of purchasing and supply be given the responsibility in conjunction with user departments and agencies for developing standard specifications for all appropriate items.
That the department of purchasing and supply develop warehousing, stocking and materials handling services across Canada for all departments other than the Department of National Defence and that a traffic advisory group be established within the new department with the responsibility of improving traffic management throughout the public service.
These and other recommendations of the Glassco commission, with the exception of the renaming of the department, have been adopted by the government, and the Department of Defence Production is now making plans for the implementation of such recommendations.
Among the other recommendations of the Glassco commission was also one which advocated the division of the department of public printing and stationery into two independent units, one to be absorbed by the proposed central purchasing agency which I have just mentioned and the other to be headed by a queen's publisher.
The government has chosen this recommendation as one of the first to be implemented and since August 21 the control of the procurement, purchasing and stores branch, the production branch and certain other of the branches of the department of
Supply-Industry
public printing and stationery has been the responsibility of the Department of Defence Production.
The queen's printer is directly responsible to me in my capacity as Minister of Industry for the publication and distribution of government documents. I consider these changes to be a significant move in line with the recommendations of the royal commission.
The proposed role of the queen's publisher involves questions of some technical complexity as well as considerations of a policy nature. This matter is now under consideration.
I should now like to outline a few of the considerations relating to the national research council. The functions of the national research council cover four broad areas:
1.	To advise the government on the position of science as a whole;
2.	To promote and encourage research in the universities;
3.	To operate a system of laboratories directed toward fundamental science and toward applied science in fields which fall outside the specific responsibilities of other government departments and agencies;
4.	To promote research in industry through the industrial research assistance program, and to give assistance through the technical information service.
In order to keep pace with its increasing responsibilities, the council has developed a continually expanding group of committees for the purpose of co-ordinating research and the various aspects of technology. At the present time the membership of such committees is approximately 3,400, drawn from the national research council itself, other federal government organizations, provincial organizations, Canadian industries and universities. This committee structure has had a most important effect on Canadian scientific co-ordination. With the expansion of research in industry it becomes particularly important to co-ordinate research undertaken by various organizations, and to make certain that all interested parties are aware of what others are doing, in so far as this may be feasible without interfering with commercial secrecy or competitive advantage.
The research council is also actively concerned with international science and, particularly in recent times, this has begun to impinge more extensively on international affairs than formerly. There are two aspects of international science: First, the benefit which Canada can obtain through her contacts with other scientific groups and, second, the co-operation which can be extended in large international undertakings such as the international geophysical year, the year of the quiet sun, the coming hydrologic decade, all

Supply-Industry
of which have yielded and will continue to yield important and useful results to all participating countries and indeed to the whole world.
To meet its obligations to foster research in Canadian universities increased expenditure will be necessary, and this can be expected to increase steadily for the foreseeable future. The graduate student population of the universities is increasing about 20 per cent per annum, and since a significant percentage of national research council grants supports these students, directly or indirectly, and since science is becoming more and more complex, requiring more expensive instrumentation, an increase of a minimum of 20 per cent is necessary merely to maintain the same level of research as that of the past fiscal year. The N.R.C. grants give university staff members an opportunity to pursue their research and to inspire an increasing number of students to proceed to advanced studies. Canada enjoys a high reputation in world science despite the fact that her expenditure on civilian science is low compared with that of most other advanced nations. In a world in which science plays a dominant role research will need increasing support if Canada is to achieve a competitive position.
The medical research council is continuing to operate as an autonomous body within the administrative framework of the national research council. It is the primary aim of the medical research council to promote the broad field of medical research in Canadian universities and their affiliated hospitals and institutes. It provides grants in aid of research projects carried out by established investigators, and as well personnel support in the form of associateships for highly qualified research workers, and fellowships for young doctors wishing to advance their research training and to provide the essential personnel for an expanding medical research program so essential for our welfare.
Increasing demands have been made on the N.R.C. applied laboratories for the benefit of Canadian industry, and over the past years the laboratories have been of assistance to many segments of industry, including the aircraft, construction, chemical, electronics and food industries, and further facilities are necessary to meet some of the demands. A new supersonic wind tunnel is nearing completion and will provide an additional facility for the aircraft industry.
The national research council library provides an important service to all segments of Canadian science, and it is being used extensively by universities and industry, and has been recognized as the major science library of Canada.

With respect to industry, the research council devotes its attention mainly to secondary industry, since the primary industries are assisted to a large extent by other government department and agencies, for example, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Forestry and the Department of Fisheries.
In the previous fiscal year, the council undertook a program to assist research in industry. This program was in effect during the latter part of the fiscal year only, but the projects initiated will, in practically all cases, be continued for the full current fiscal year. As a result of this the new applications anticipated, a substantial increase in the vote is necessary if the program is to be continued at an effective level.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at length at this particular stage of the discussion of the estimates, but from considerable experience in the House of Commons I realize that it is necessary to record dissent at certain times; otherwise later on someone will rise and say that no one objected to a certain course of action, and we will be pursuing the matter again. Therefore I now record my dissent to this method of dealing with a large number of estimates under the Department of Industry. I understand the circumstances which have brought this about, but I want to make it clear that in the next session of parliament we would ask for the estimates under this minister to be taken in a different way. Rather than have a comprehensive statement by the minister covering the five or six areas for which he is responsible, we would prefer to revert to the practice which has prevailed in the past of taking these matters separately, so that debate on each area of responsibility is related directly to the estimates under consideration. We are in some difficulty here tonight. Various hon. members may wish to speak on any one of these half dozen items and we may get the debate rather mixed up, just as the minister's statement was a cumulative effort.
The reason we are going to be helpful to the minister is simply because we know that on interim supply which was in front of us today, the government is requesting money for the ninth month in the fiscal year. In other words, three quarters of the total amount of money required to operate government institutions and efforts will be voted by the house through the method of interim supply. It is rather pointless then to deal with the estimates item by item, scrutinizing every single dollar of expenditure, when nine twelfths already has been expended.

The other consideration is that as a responsible official opposition we are interested in bringing this session to a close before the Christmas recess. We are not taking the attitude or the stand which was taken by the irresponsible official opposition of last year which refused to pass a single estimate of the estimates which were placed before it. So in that co-operative mood, all I am doing now is making sure that our position in the next session will not be misunderstood, and we would ask at that time that the Minister of Industry deal with his estimates for the Department of Industry and let the house comment on them, then move on to defence production with appropriate comments, and then the other items which he has under his authority.
Let me say I fully appreciate his difficulties. He has so many departments or crown companies to supervise that he is a thoroughly overburdened minister of the crown. I went through that myself, Mr. Chairman, with the duties of atomic energy, national research council, medical research council, at one time Eldorado, over and above the Department of Trade and Commerce. Superimposed on that were my government house leader duties, and I have forgotten what other problems were shifted to my shoulders. So I sympathize with this minister who has obviously become the workhorse of the present Liberal government.
So far as the Department of Industry is concerned, the estimates there are the only ones which are new, brought in by way of a supplementary estimate. We presented in this house our objection to the setting up of that Department of Industry. We had rather an extensive debate on it at the time, and we are still not very happy with regard to that arrangement. A very prominent businessman suggested to one of my colleagues the other day that the minute we again resume office -and he is a Liberal and anticipates this event-we should abolish the Department of Industry and put the field it encompasses back where it belongs, under the Department of Trade and Commerce; so we will take that under advisement.
As I say, some of our members will be speaking about the Department of Industry. I thought the minister should have continued immediately with defence production when he had finished with his department, but he interposed the atomic energy field between those two and then came along with national research. It is unfortunate to mix them up like this. If I get the opportunity later this evening, I may have something to say with regard to atomic energy and national research, and I will particularly ask the minister
Supply-Industry
some questions with regard to those fields of activity. With regard to the medical research council, he might as well have ready an answer to the question whether or not he is going to bring in legislation next session concerning the council, because that was one of the plans we had under way. We have been given a mixed bag to deal with. I do not intend at this stage to talk about these things seriatim. I merely indicate and record permanently on record in Hansard my dissent from this method of dealing with these estimates.

speechtext:
Some remarks have been made about the loyalty of the civil service. Now we can see it.
The subjects of the Department of Industry have been debated so much this session that it is difficult to find anything new and relevant to say, but I would draw the attention of the committee to something which happened in my own area-something which I thought was bound to happen. There is now a concerted effort by the industrial and municipal groups in our area to be classified as a designated area, despite the fact that the formula, about which I have complained earlier, will not qualify the area to become so designated, at least not for several more years when conditions have got a great deal worse than they are now. The Minister of Finance told us a few weeks ago that certain adjustments to this formula were being considered and that more variables would be taken into account. I would like to have been given more information about this. I read the text of the speech the minister made last Friday and I do not recall he had anything to say about this aspect of the matter. I am sure there are other places, in addition to northwest Ontario which are beginning to stew about this question. The gist of the request is: why cannot we share in these advantages which are to come from the establishment of the Department of Industry and the tax concessions which are to be made? Advertisements for personnel to staff

Supply-Industry
the department have appeared in papers across the country. I know, having gone through the newspapers in the reading room, that a considerable bill for advertising has been incurred. I have seen at least five or six editorials in small papers commenting on these advertisements, the salaries offered, the qualifications desired, and so on.
To my mind, a certain puzzlement has arisen, one which the pamphlet which has been published cannot answer. How are these officials to work, and what administrative framework is to be set up? I know the deputy minister has been making speeches in various places, because I have seen the reports. I know the minister has commented on the reaction of Manitoba to the Department of Industry. I do not know how much truth there is in this, but I hear there was a blowup or at least some criticism expressed at the federal-provincial conference on the subject of the department after the minister had made his explanation. I understand the minister had a pitched battle in one of the corridors with Mr. Eric Kierans of the province of Quebec. That is just tittle-tattle, but I am sure of this: The Department of Industry and its policies have been the subject of discussion and explanation while the provincial ministers have been down here. I think we should be brought up to date as to those discussions and be told what response the minister received. I assume, since he has not been here in the house so much this week, that he has been attending the conference and, knowing him, I assume he has not been sitting there like a dummy without making any contribution.
Like many other people, the minister must, I am sure, realize that his new Department of Industry is in a somewhat precarious position in terms of general acceptance, or in terms of popularity, and the sooner its function is clarified and popularized, the sooner we see some evidence of people out in the field working with the local regional development groups, the more quickly will it be able to perform those tasks which we can expect it to perform. With regard to what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre to the effect that if and when the Conservatives came back to power they would abolish the department, I am sure we were reminded of what Ross Thatcher was going to do about medicare. If the department gets running and functioning well, we shall not have to worry about any subsequent government destroying it.
The main question asked in my region and by the people I encountered in Manitoba and southwestern Ontario about the Department of Industry is a simple one: How is it going to work with the provincial groups

which are already in existence; how much flexibility will there be in this relationship? The main problem seems to be this: Who will take the lead? We all know the steps which have been taken by Manitoba and I am sure we shall hear more about them, because I see the hon. member for Marquette is there with that massive volume about Manitoba's plan between 1962 and 1975. What is to be done in Ontario? What is to be the relationship with the regional development councils and the development associations in the various provinces? When are we to be given some idea as to the degree of initiative which is to come from the provinces and from the federal government in terms of projects. This is important.
We saw what I think was the best piece of legislation passed by the former government, that is, the ARDA legislation, lying on the counter for a long time before it was picked up. There was, and still is, a great deal of confusion in many parts of the country about what could be done with ARDA. There was uncertainty about its implementation. I know a period of more than two years passed in Ontario before Mr. H. F. Crown was appointed by the provincial government, and a response was forthcoming from the province. It is still not certain, as far as ARDA is concerned, whether the initiative should come from regional groups or from the provinces, or whether it is for the federal government to take the initiative. Indeed, I am confident, from what I know of ARDA operations, that all those concerned are still hazy about it. I suggest to the minister that he will not be able to afford the maturity period which ARDA has been allowed. I say this because I think the pressures in this area, where employment is concerned, are much sharper in the case of the new department. This is why I would have appreciated-I will not say "more candour", because it is not easy to see how there could be much more candour when there is nothing to be candid about-but I would have appreciated more detail about how the process of building up the department is going on. How many men has the minister hired? What is their quality? Where did he stand in the competition? Where are the advisory offices to be established? What research assistance is to be available to the outer offices?
Information of this kind would be important and useful. It would have a definite bearing on the department's future. I know the deputy minister has been speaking about this in Ottawa but the reports are in general terms. I think some of this information might be given in greater detail during this debate.
The next thing I wanted to touch on is something that is dear to my heart, as the minister knows, and that is the question of

government printing and publishing. It has always been my suspicion since I arrived in Ottawa some years ago that this is one of the least efficient operations of the government. Most of us remember the reckless doings of the public accounts committee a few years ago when they were turning up trout streams in the basement of the establishment in Hull, and we had all kinds of cynicism and bitter wit about the place. Subsequently, we had a change in the headship over there and things quieted down considerably.
It seems to me, as a matter of principle, that there needs to be an element of contract letting in so far as printing is concerned. I am speaking for my party here when I say that we are not so much dedicated to the socialistic idea that we want to see all the printing done for the federal government-particularly I am thinking of text print-handled by the queen's printer. I can see the advantages of a balance, but I can also see the possibility of patronage and pettiness in so far as the letting of contracts is concerned. I know from my personal knowledge that there was one magazine put out for the Canadian army, and as soon as the government changed a few years ago, slam bang, the printing contract was shifted to someone favourable to the party in power. We may have an element of this; but forgetting that sort of thing it seems to me that what we have to look for in that kind of contracting is the absolute in competition, with favouritism ruled out. I am not so sure that we have it. I should like more details on how this print purchasing is going to be carried out, to be sure that under the reforms the minister is introducing we will have this as a guarantee.
The next point in connection with the queen's printer's operations relates to something that has exercised me for six years, and that is the fact that all of these small contracts for materials and goods that I think run to something like $18 million a year, have always been concentrated in this particular area, that is in the Ottawa-Montreal-Toronto triangle. There has not been nearly enough dispersal out across the country. We have had suggestions of this over the past years which showed, particularly in 1960-61, that there was an attempt made to spread these orders out. Almost anywhere I have gone across Canada the printers, suppliers of forms and so on, even in the smallest towns, feel they could compete or should have the right to bid on this kind of order. Yet, in fact, the small orders which these people could fill seem to be given to a very select group in this particular triangle. I
Supply-Industry
should like to bring this to the minister's attention in the hope that it will be his aim to improve the situation. I do not believe the Glassco report makes the situation clear as to whether more purchasing in this category could be made in the provinces beyond Ontario and Quebec.
The minister will also be aware from some of the questions which I placed, and which he answered, that there is a tremendous amount of initiative put in the hands of the man who is in charge of this kind of purchasing. It is the kind of initiative that has to be handled with scrupulous fairness. There is too much power, in a sense, placed in the hands of someone purchasing that much in the way of supplies in a year, unless the rules and the code are very strict. In time, the man at the top of the organization has the right, which is exercised and I think the minister will concede that it has been exercised to a considerable extent, to change orders, to change the number of competitors, to call for new bids or to have telephone calls go out to get quotations from the select people. You have here the opportunity for corruption and unfairness.
I think that if the minister could say that under the new procedures that are going to be developed under the Department of Defence Production this situation will be taken care of, I will be pleased and I know several other members in this house who will be pleased. This particular community of Ottawa and Hull is a great place to generate rumours and suspicions. I do not want to go into the information that has been brought to me. I am willing to accept the minister's integrity in this matter, but I should like to have along with that general assurance something of the details that are planned for this kind of purchasing.
Then, I should like to point out to the minister that there is a bit of discrepancy in some of the answers that were given to me. I will just give him an example. I should like to refer to question No. 1,286, on page 3623 of Hansard for October 16, 1963, which reads in part as follows:
Has Mr. Roger Duhamel, the queen's printer, been offered the proposed post of queen's publisher and, if so, (a) has he accepted (b) will his salary remain unchanged (c) what are his major responsibilities (d) to whom is he immediately responsible, and (e) on what date did he first act in an acting capacity?
The answer given by the minister is as follows:
The creation of the proposed post of queen's publisher and the related changes in legislation are still under consideration.

This has all been assumed by and put directly under the Department of Defence Production. The queen's printer, in relation to his proposed functions, or functions suggested by the royal commission on reorganization, is to become the queen's publisher, and is in fact performing now these more specialized duties, of rather more than an editorial nature than the previous mechanical ones were, but the title has not yet been approved. The title has not been assumed and if inadvertently-and 1 suggest it was inadvertently-the answer was given that the queen's publisher had done something, it was taken to mean the queen's printer had done it in his new capacity.

Well, we will be interested and looking forward to the appointment of

the queen's publisher, and the definition of his duties, when that develops.
I have mentioned the Bobcat to the minister. I remember it was four and a half years ago when Fort William was dreaming of getting an actual contract for the Bobcat, and at that time the development contract for it was with the Canadian Car Company in Montreal. I remember attending on a delegation here which was met by the Hon. Howard Green, and I remember the deputy minister being asked point blank by Mr. Green how long it would be before the contract would be ready for awarding, that is, when the decision would be made that the Bobcat was worth producing.
As I remember it, the deputy minister took some care in answering, because I imagine this is not the kind of thing a person likes to get on the line for; but there was further insistence and he then came up with the figure of 18 months. In other words, approximately three years ago the thing should have been ready to go out to contract, but the defence committee apparently has been told there are still bugs in the Bobcat, and this is three years after the estimate made by the deputy minister.
Through all the years since then there has been an item in the estimates for the development work, but there must be something badly wrong or haywire about the situation, about the kind of ineffective leadership coming from the department, particularly when something fumbles and bumbles along like this. I know the one conclusion I draw from a defence point of view is that much of our defence posture is nonsense, because obviously if we can afford to fritter away years like that before we get an armoured carrier, we really don't care a damn whether we get an armoured carrier or not.
My point is that the minister needs to give some explanation of how this could take place under an efficient department. It does not make sense to me that four and a half years ago we got an undertaking it would be ready for contract in 18 months, and there was an indication given that favourable consideration would be given to Fort William. In fact I remember the headlines in the Fort William and Port Arthur press saying, "We are going to get 400 Bobcats to build in a year and a half." It has now become less than a joke; it is just a wry irony.
How can this take place under any kind of efficient direction by a government department? Has part of the stalling been that the government has been trying to get cooperation with some of our NATO allies on this matter? I know that the other day the Minister of Defence Production sent me a photograph of the Bobcat, with some British

officers looking at it. I suppose there has never been an armoured vehicle looked at and examined so much as the Bobcat, but ten years after it was first talked about we still have not got anything except a nice bill.
One of my colleagues tells me the United States and United Kingdom now have their own vehicles. I do not know about that, but it is quite obvious they do not go for the Canadian vehicle. It also seems to me there is no use trying to fasten it in any political sense on the former Liberal government or the former Conservative government. There is just something completely haywire, and it is this kind of thing which makes one wonder how good is the Department of Defence Production.
I have my own specific case in connection with the Department of Defence Production which I would like to go into tonight, but since it is still under review I will not. It relates to a contract in my own area, which convinces me this is not the greatest of departments; but this Bobcat business is just unbelievable. For 10 years we have been fiddling around trying to get an armoured carrier for Canadian troops, and the latest results show it is still not worth very much. I am not surprised that the Americans and British are not anxious to take up any of our creations, inventions or developments, if this is the pattern.
We have never had a clear explanation of it, and I think the minister should tell us about it. We have spent millions of dollars on the development program. I am sure it supplied work, though not very much because there are only about 20 prototypes, but a lot was spent on materials, and it made work for engineers and a small staff in the Canadian Car Company in Montreal. Surely we should have some explanation from the minister before his estimates are passed.
It also seems to me that the minister should tell us more about the aircraft problems we have-that is, the problems of selling our aircraft to some of our allies under the defence program. It is quite apparent that the CL-44 is a successful aircraft, but it has not yet met with great purchasing responses by other countries for defence purposes. I would like to know the reason for this, particularly with regard to that aircraft, because greater production of it would do something for Montreal, which has been bleating so much over the DC-9, and also particularly because of the fact that an adaptation of it was taken for our air force, and I understand is in use.
We need to know more about the responsibility of the department in helping to get sales contracts for that particular aircraft, and I would like to know something about

whatever funds the department may have contributed in connection with the cushion aircraft-you know, the flying saucer type, and also in connection with the hydrofoils, I would like to know if there is any program under which the Department of Defence Production is contributing money for research services and development. I understand we have been experimenting with hydrofoils ever since Casey Baldwin was fooling around with one in Nova Scotia 30 years ago; but if the same pattern prevails as with the Bobcat, I can see us still fiddling around with hydrofoils in 2000 A.D.
The next point I want to touch on is related to the national research council and the role that it plays as the encourager or the leader in the field of science. I have a paper here by W. P. Thompson entitled "The number of university teachers: needs and prospects". Dr. Thompson was formerly the head of the University of Saskatchewan and was the author of a book called "Graduate education in the sciences in Canadian universities" published by the University of Toronto Press in 1963. This paper is for publication in the December issue of the Canadian Association of University Teachers Bulletin. I do not want to put a great deal of it on the record, but in substance Dean Thompson is telling us that our graduate program-that is, the program to produce graduates, particularly with Ph.D's-in the social sciences and the humanities is in a hopeless position. It is just fantastic that a country with this many people in universities should be turning out so few graduates in these fields. There is in this paper a table of the number of theses accepted for doctorate in different subjects in different Canadian universities in 1960-61. One of the interesting things is that in the sciences we have 151 theses accepted; in medicine, agriculture and engineering-which is another type of science -we have 53. But when we get into the social subjects we have a total of only 68. When we get into the humanities we have a total of only 51.
This is not the place to make an argument for the social sciences and the humanities, but I would suggest that even the record in the sciences of only 151 in biology, chemistry, geology, mathematics and physics is a pretty weak effort. The national research council needs even more encouragement than it is getting at the present time in order to broaden this program. I know the minister indicated this was so; but what is the scale of this, what is the imagination, what are we shooting for, how many hundred graduates a year

Supply-Industry
can N.R.C. sponsor? This is what we need to know. I wish to quote from page 4 of Dean Thompson's paper:
Disregarding the applied subjects for the moment-
That is, the applied sciences:
-the number of teachers who will be required in the basic sciences in relation to those in the social subjects and humanities cannot be determined accurately by estimating the number of students registered in the different faculties, since students in each type of faculty take varying amounts of work in the other faculties. But a reasonably accurate comparison may be made by comparing the numbers of present faculty members. An examination of the lists of teachers in several universities which have typical establishments of faculties shows that the present numbers of teachers above the level of part time sessional appointees are approximately the same in the basic sciences as in the social subjects and in the humanities (for example, in one institution 7:6:8). Therefore, the number of doctorates actually conferred in the sciences is out of all proportion to those in other areas-three to one instead of one to one.
In this connection it should be pointed out that six of the 13 universities which conferred the doctorate did so only in the sciences, and that two others conferred only one or two doctorates in all the other subjects put together. Apparently only five institutions-
That is institutions in Canada:
-make any serious effort to carry students through the doctorate in the social subjects or humanities. Although only 13 institutions conferred the degree in 1960-61, 15 offer work leading to the degree, but two made no awards in that year. Those two offer the degree only in the sciences.
The reason for the great disproportion cannot be a matter of cost since research and advance teaching in the sciences are much more costly than in other areas, although it must be admitted that more money may be available for scientists from outside sources. Other possible reasons may be suggested for consideration: (1) a difference in the number of suitable fellowships and assistant-ships; (2) an established tradition owing to the greater number and variety of subsequent jobs hitherto available; (3) less interest on the part of many social scientists and humanists than on the part of natural scientists in original scholarly work; (4) less inspiration to their students to proceed to graduate work at the doctoral level. At any rate it appears that the attitude of many scientists must be different from that of many nonscientists and that the difference is recognized in general university policies.
This might be taken as an argument-

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. This paper continues:
Even though the doctorates in the natural sciences greatly outnumber those in other areas, it is clear that even they are far short of the need. Mathematics is an especially weak spot with only eight, although mathematicians are in great demand. Moreover, a large percentage of fresh Ph.D.'s in the sciences go into industry, the professions, or government service. Precise information on this point comes from two sources: (1) according to Thompson, the deans of graduate schools estimate that less than 20 per cent of Ph.D.'s in chemistry, 33 per cent in physics, 5 per cent in geology, and 50 per cent in biology join university staffs; (2) Stock and Beaulieu showed that of the science students who received their Ph.D.'s in 1960 and immediately took jobs, only 27 per cent joined university staffs, 23 per cent went into government service, 23 per cent into other occupations in Canada, and 26 per cent into various kinds of employment in other countries. Twenty eight per cent of all science students who received the Ph.D. in that year did not take employment at once but continued their studies at the post-doctoral level.
The evidence Dr. Thompson introduces here suggests that the sciences are in better shape than the social sciences and the humanities in having people capable of university work. I think the N.R.C. deserves a great deal of credit in this regard. Those of us who are not interested so much in the sciences lament that we have not a comparable body-at least, I do not think the Canada Council is yet. But the point is, even this is not very good, and it seems to me that the N.R.C. needs to give even more leadership and opportunities for post-doctoral work and pre-doctoral work, and there should be a more aggressive program, particularly in providing the kind of research projects that will keep that 26 per cent-which I think is a fair average-who go every year to other countries because they can get greater research opportunities in terms of projects and funds. I would ask the minister and the N.R.C. to let us know just how big they are thinking, and I would encourage them to think big in this kind of program.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate I have no intention of delaying the estimates of the minister. I only wish to put on record some thoughts in connection with the Department of Industry. The minister has so many irons in the fire that it would be futile to attempt to discuss all the matters which fall within his jurisdiction; but the Department of Industry is a subject of wide discussion and criticism across the land. I agree that probably it is practical to put under one roof various activities that are related but in the words of an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of October 28 under the heading "A Pretty-Costly Beginning," it states:

Whatever else might be said about the federal government's new Department of Industry, there is no doubt that it is going to Think Big.
Well, it thinks big; it talks big, but whether we will get big results time alone will tell.
The Department of Industry was created by parliament in the same manner as was the case with other legislative enactments that have been passed since this session of parliament opened. The government has the habit of putting the cart before the horse. It leaps before it comes to the stile. It makes a decision and then it decides to consult those who are most vitally concerned.
The province of Manitoba in particular is greatly concerned. That province was not consulted. That province, which has such an efficiently working department of industry, should have been consulted or at least kept aware of what Ottawa intended to do. But the government has acted in the same way as it did with the municipal loan fund and contributory pensions. They put the legislation on the books and then they start to consult. I believe consultation was promised the members of the government of Manitoba at the federal-provincial conference. Whether consultation on this point was carried out, we do not know. However, the Winnipeg Tribune of October 19 has this comment by the premier of Manitoba:
Premier Duff Roblin likened the new Department of Industry to "the pension muddle".
Premier Roblin is disturbed and fears there will be duplication and confusion with regard to industrial surveys which this department will be making, trade missions it may be sending overseas and personnel it may be be hiring. The minister of industry of Manitoba, the Hon. Gurney Evans, is quoted in the same issue of the Winnipeg Tribune as saying:
-the present course "seemed to be one of building two competing empires".
Why is Manitoba disturbed? I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the government of Manitoba under the leadership of the Hon. Duff Roblin spent three-quarters of a million dollars making an economic survey in that province. The result of that survey is this monumental volume I hold in my hand. I draw it to the attention of the minister and I suggest that those high priced officials who are being sought in this little pamphlet issued by the civil service commission the other day be told to read and study this monumental volume, because it covers every field of economic activity. I want to point out to the minister that it covers Manitoba, an economy in transition, population and manpower, primary industries, secondary manufacturing industries, prime requisites for industrial
Supply-Industry
development, tourism, recreational development and accommodation, service industries, physical factors in economic growth, capital requirements and taxation, social factors and economic growth.
This is a most exhaustive study and it will be well worth while for the new Department of Industry to make a thorough study of it and save the thousands and thousands of dollars that would be required to make an economic survey of the province of Manitoba. I do not know what the situation is in other provinces, but as far as Manitoba is concerned this study is most exhaustive. I want to put on record how it came about.
In 1961 the government of the Hon. Duff Roblin realized that job opportunities were not keeping up with the number of candidates in the labour field. There were more workers than there were jobs. Consequently the government budgeted three quarters of a million dollars to start a survey. They initiated a committee on Manitoba's economic future consisting of 42 members. They hired consultants from various parts of Canada and the United States and 200 public spirited citizens of the province also banded together voluntarily to help to make this great survey of the whole province. The recommendations contained herein were made by representatives of labour, primary producers, educationists, professional men and government officials. In this volume the minister will find how to increase job opportunities at least in the province of Manitoba, if in no other.
I wish to return to the comments in the Free Press, the mouthpiece of the Liberal party in Manitoba. In the issue of October 28 last there is an editorial which indicates that the Free Press is greatly disturbed. It points out that 300 top jobs are being created and that the civil service commission is carrying on a recruitment program and offering top salaries from $12,000 to $17,000 a year. Premier Roblin is quite disturbed by the fact that many of those working in the Manitoba department of industry may be enticed to join the federal Department of Industry because of the salaries being offered. There was no consultation even on that point.
This same Free Press editorial questions what industrial activities will be launched by virtue of the establishment of the Department of Industry and the employment of around 300 top level people. What new industrial activities are going to be launched to justify the establishment of this department? I think the minister should be given the opportunity to answer that question when he replies, so as to alleviate the anxiety that some people, even those who support his party, feel about the whole matter.

Supply-Industry
The editorial in the Free Press goes on to say that the Department of Industry will have to create $100 million in new investment each year to justify its existence. Was any thought ever given to that? I should like to quote the last paragraph of the editorial:
The first 300 executives, however, are only the start. The department hopes to double that number in time. All in all, the new men of the Department of Industry are going to have to produce some pretty substantial results to earn their keep. Canadians who, heaven knows, recognize the need for industrial development will wish them luck but also hope that the government in its enthusiasm does not forget its obligation to make offsetting economies elsewhere in the public service.
I submit this for consideration by the minister. I hope he gives us some answers as to the new field of endeavour he intends to enter with this army of personnel being advertised for at high salaries. I, like everyone else, have been very interested in this pamphlet entitled "Department of Industry" issued by the civil service commission. It sets out the qualifications required of various officials. In particular it refers to the department's functions and organizations. I was interested in its responsibilities at the management level. It first of all refers to the establishment and maintenance of liaison with industries, and the acquisition of information covering all aspects of their activities. I take it that the department intends to establish liaison, not only with large industries which are established in the east in Ontario and Quebec, but also with small industries established out west. The pamphlet says:
-to plan, conduct and implement comprehensive studies.. .to provide advice and assistance in the establishment of new manufacturing facilities and in the growth and improvement of those already in existence.
In this connection I have another question for the minister: Is he going to give any attention to industries already in existence, large or small? I have in mind industries such as have been established in Minnedosa, at Carberry, at Sprague, and other places, through the effects of this active Manitoba department of industry.
I am also particularly interested in an industry in my own riding. Minnedosa is a small town, as small towns are measured in the east. It is in an agricultural area and has about 3,000 population. It found itself in difficulty several years ago owing to the fact that the repair shops of the C.P.R. in the town were closed down. Some enterprising citizens made a survey of the possibilities of finding employment and a company was organized called Minn-Toba Industries, Ltd. As a result of the survey they decided to manufacture tractor and combine cabs-

everyone connected with agriculture knows what they are-and short-line farm equipment. This company has organized and was assisted by the industrial development board of Manitoba, some $10 million being set aside by the board, for cases like this, to assist small industries setting themselves up. They started to manufacture these implements in 1961 and employed as many as 52 men. That, of course, means 52 wives, and if you multiply that by three it means the feeding of 250 people.
These tractor and combine cabs proved to be of superior design to, and better workmanship than, those brought in from the United States. As a result of the survey it was discovered that there was a tariff against United States imports of tractor and combine cabs. Once this company was nicely established a network of distributorships was set up and the company carried on on a straight business basis. Then bang, the tariff on United States tractor and combine cabs was removed. When this company Minn-Toba Industries Ltd., set out to see what business they could get in the United States, they found that the tariff against Canadian-manufactured tractor and combine cabs was 20 per cent. This particular industry employed last April 52 men. By August this number was cut to half, production of these cabs cut to one-third, and all because United States manufactured cabs are imported duty free by our large implement companies in Ontario. They give distribution discounts and are knocking this little industry, which meant so much to that town, out of existence.
My suggestion is this. If the Minister of Industry intends to justify his position and that of his officials, he may have to co-operate with the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance to this extent. We are asking-probably there are other small industries in Canada who are in the same plight also-that we clamp a tariff duty on United States imports, a like duty of 20 per cent, taking the matter up with the tariff board or the powers that be, or else asking the United States to remove the tariff on our tractor and combine cabs so that they can enter the United States and compete with the United States product.
All that we and our industries want is fair play. If the Department of Industry is going to direct its activities toward helping even the small industries, I say it justifies its existence. But it should explain at once what it intends to do so as to allay any fears which may be in the minds of provincial governments, and so on. I do not blame the minister for not consulting other provincial governments on this score because he is only

one member of the government. As I said in my introductory remarks, the government decides first of all to pass legislation, and then secondly enter into consultation. I hope the minister and his department will cooperate in this regard. When public money has already been spent let us take advantage of it. I repeat that I hope the minister sets his personnel the task of studying this large report, which is bigger than a family bible, consisting of hundreds of pages. It is in great detail and is worthy of consideration. But do not forget the small industries. If the minister's colleagues co-operate with him to see that our little industries get fair play, that is all I am asking tonight.

Mr. Chairman, before I make my speech, it is my painful task to announce that an awful air tragedy has just happened. A T.C.A. airliner carrying 111 passengers and a crew of 7 has just crashed 20 miles out of Montreal. News of that terrible accident has just come in and I wanted to communicate the information to the house.
Now, Mr. Chairman, since we are considering the estimates of the Department of Industry, I should like to express the views of the Social Credit party on that subject.
First of all, I take the liberty to congratulate very warmly the minister who was chosen to fill that post. He is perfectly bilingual, has a great experience in administrative matters and is highly qualified in industry and business. I feel also that the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) is able to direct his department masterfully. However, knowing the government's good intentions, in words at least, with regard to bilingualism, I was very surprised to notice that out of 14 officials appointed to his department to date, only two have French names and I am asking myself: Are all the high officials bilingual?
When creating this new department, the government had a unique occasion to show publicly to Canada that it is serious about bilingualism.
Mr. Chairman, the function of the Department of Industry is no doubt to work closely with the provinces, the municipalities and the area industrial promotion organizations, etc., in order to promote and facilitate the creation of new processing industries throughout Canada and particularly in depressed areas.
Canada needs diversified and decentralized manufacturing industries. Industrial concentration is responsible for excessive growth in some areas of the country and pernicious anemia in others. That occasion should be taken to destroy that clever illusion or myth which has been kept alive in public opinion
Supply-Industry
those last few years, namely that being far from great consumption centres was for some areas an obstacle to industrial expansion.
In that case, not one industry would be suitably located in relation to domestic and foreign markets. When a company manufactures a product of good quality which can prove useful to the consumer, it will sell anywhere and the geographical location of the industry has nothing to do with it. In proof of this, one only has to look at the shelves in shops and wholesalers' warehouses and check the origin of the great variety of goods, to realize that they come from every part of Canada and from approximately 50 foreign countries with which we transact business regularly.
We should also do away with the fable spread by certain representatives who advocate the merger of medium-sized industries, claiming that only the big industry can survive in our times. Such an attitude can kill resourcefulness and discourage those who are bold and determined enough to set up a business. The survival of industry does not lie in concentration or merger. Those are false arguments inspired by socialism.
Beside large businesses, there is room for the medium and the small industry, that is undertakings in keeping with the abilities of man. To that effect, we should not be afraid to consider new solutions. We should free public capital-governments, municipalities, school boards-to direct them in industrial and commercial investments, in order to ensure an unlimited development of the national economy by establishing a public credit bank which would be a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada.
On the other hand, the industrial development bank should guarantee, after the required authorizations, the issue of industrial and commercial bonds, in order to ensure complete security of private savings from any source whatever, and enable Canadians to regain control of their economy. Moreover, the exchange fund, to facilitate the international exchange of goods and services, should accept in its reserves the monetary units of many countries, that is currencies not convertible into gold, which would result in settling the problem of international payments and increasing considerably our foreign trade.
We must go still farther to get out of this inflationary debt-money financial system of ours, which makes debts and taxes go up and interferes with the economic activity in Canada.
It is the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), the national leader of the Social Credit party, who was stating at Orleans on November 28 last that chartered banks had extended or created $1,200 million

Supply-Industry
dollars worth of new credit in 1962, on which 6 per cent had to be paid, or an amount of $70,000,000 in interests only, that is $17.50 annually for each family, and that indefinitely.
Mr. Chairman, with the new Department of Industry, the national production should show a substantial increase; but if the government thinks it will thus solve the unemployment problem, it is greatly mistaken, for the consumers or the families of Canada, in a proportion close to one third, do not have the means to buy present production. Already, our national production will hit the $44.6 billion mark. Our money has no value, because of inflation, and it is impossible to buy the whole present production.
Is it not the beloved martyr, President John F. Kennedy, who said last September that the most important task facing the United States was that of the monetary reform?
New President Lyndon B. Johnson dealt with that subject when he stated the following, as reported in Le Devoir, Wednesday, November 27:
And second, no act ot ours could more fittingly continue the work of President Kennedy than the earliest passage of the tax bill (which would bring about a tax reduction of $11 billion) for which he fought, a bill designed to increase our national income, our federal revenues, and our insurance against recession.
Without the monetary reform advocated by the Social Credit, it will be impossible to create a constant economic prosperity keeping pace with the population growth in Canada.
As the minister said a moment ago, the number of university students increases at a rate of 20 per cent every year. If we add to this number all those who are in secondary schools, how shall we succeed in employing all the new manpower coming regularly on the labour market?
Mr. Chairman, I cannot deal with industrial development without calling the attention of the Minister of Industry to my own riding of Chicoutimi and the Saguenay area. The riding of Chicoutimi is divided into two depressed areas: Chicoutimi and Port Alfred. Special care is required for this area, because 27 per cent of its population depend on unemployment insurance or welfare assistance.
There is in Chicoutimi an important industry that could be brought back to life with the co-operation of the Quebec government.
I know that the minister, in a speech delivered here in Ottawa, said that he would cooperate with the Department of Industry in the various provinces. That would be a wonderful occasion to bring back to life industries closed since 1930 and to put to work again assets worth $20 million which lie idle now. A regional economic planning

council was set up last October whose primary object is to promote industrial expansion. I feel that good relations must be created to facilitate industrial promotion.
In Chicoutimi North, my home town, an industrial and commercial exhibition was recently held and was a great success. The industrial board of that city helped three new minor industries to re-enter business during the past year.
We are trying presently to create an industrial spirit in our area. Our ports: Bagotville, Port Alfred, Chicoutimi, and even L'Anse Saint-Jean, are open gateways on the whole world. Those places are even the major ports in Canada for shipping the raw materials we have, and with all the industrial facilities at our disposal, there is every possibility for a very intensive industrial development.
Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will give particular attention to the few points I have outlined, for we need the help of the Department of Industry, which has just been created, to promote industrial development and allow our families to live decently.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to add my words of congratulation to the minister on his appointment to this lofty post and on the very efficient way that he has been carrying out his duties in that capacity. I may say that the very fast way in which he has commenced the operation of this department might indicate that the comparison that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre made is not an entirely correct one, since he called him the workhorse of the cabinet. I suggest that his present pace might indicate he is built along speedier lines. He might well turn out to be the Man-o'-War of the cabinet, rather than the mere cumbersome Clydesdale. No matter how it turns out, Mr. Chairman, I am sure that at the end of the race he will pay off across the board for the party I represent.
Now, having passed these few equine bouquets, I trust I will not do what hon. gentlemen opposite do so often when they pass bouquets, that is take them away again before the minister gets a chance to put them in the flower pot. I have a few words I should like to say on behalf of my constituents with regard to this department, and that is the purpose for which I believe I was sent here by my constituents.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in the creation of the new Department of Industry the minister has a very great opportunity to remedy some of the defects in the department as it existed before, that is the Department of Defence Production. As I understand it, the Department of Defence Production grew

up very largely, and certainly came to maturity, during the war years and the immediate post-war boom years. I suggest that in the process it may be that the department, which played a large part in the economic life of so many of our industries, lost sight of the fact that, being a department of government it was something more than just an agency of business. It should have been operated in a different way from a business organization, and as a department of government it surely had a very great social purpose which industry in the private sphere does not have to entertain.
I suggest that possibly in the past, from time to time, the Department of Defence Production as it has been operated has lost sight of any social purpose, as it must have if it has any raison d'etre as a government department or as a government agency. I suggest that possibly at times, particularly in its buying aspects, the Department of Defence Production lost sight of its social purpose and operated purely as a private business on a dollars and cents basis. I suggest that for a government department this might not be entirely correct. I hope that the minister, in conceiving the road and direction which this new Department of Industry is to walk, will consider not only efficiency, not only the cheapest way to buy, but will also consider the social ramifications to various parts of Canada in the various operating policies and in the directions the new department is going to take.
It is obvious that the department to date, at least the Department of Defence Production, has been very largely concerned in the aircraft and electronics fields. If in those areas there is to be bidding for contracts, and if there is to be no delimitation of any kind on that bidding, if there are not going to be certain preferences for small industries, certain areas where only small industry is allowed to bid or certain areas where industries that are particularly suited to a locality are allowed to bid, then surely the big are going to get bigger and there is going to be no room at all for the small. If this takes place the consequences will be that the big will have the field to themselves, and I suggest that in the long run this will redound to the detriment of the Canadian taxpayer.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in the formation of the philosophies and the policies of the new department there should be a very careful look, not just at the dollars and cents aspect, not just at the big business aspect, but at the aspect of what is best for Canada. Because behind the very theory of the Department of Industry there is surely the idea,
Supply-Industry
as is indicated by the fact that designated areas have been appointed-there is, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam stated today, the very idea on which Canada is founded, namely that there must be some equality between the rich and the poor, that all must not go to the few and none to the many. I think this not only applies as to provinces between themselves but surely as to the citizens and workers of Canada also.
Therefore I suggest there should be areas within the department, and within the bidding practices of the department, that will be reserved to the small industries, to the encouragement and growth of industries that we wish to develop; and in particular, on occasion if certain industries are well adapted to a certain area, then surely the buying practices of a government department such as this should lend themselves to the encouragement and development of these industries. They should not be left out in the cold and cruel marketplace, where sometimes the methods and techniques of the giants of industry make it impossible for the small to compete.
I cite but one small example of this, and while this is not pervasive it is a fact, that certainly in the electronics industry there are subsidiaries of large industries who make components, which will ultimately go into a contract the department is bidding on; and I am given to understand that if a subsidiary is bidding on certain contracts, then the parent company, in giving prices to other tenderers, may charge them a great deal more for those parts than they charge to their own subsidiary. This puts any other bidder right out of competition.
I do not know how actively the old department of defence production looked into this type of practice, but certainly in the United States there has been an area of great concern that monopolies and combinations in industry, interlocking directorships and so on, would render it impossible for the small and new industry to compete. I hope in the buying practices of the department in the future there will be great concern in the new department, not only to ascertain that the bidding practices of the big make the game fair for the small, but also that the department will definitely have it as a policy that it will encourage the growth of small and new industries in the electronics and allied aircraft field, so that it will not just be a feeding ground for those industries which are already large and well established.
In this regard, in my constituency we have such industries that have developed with hardship in this type of a difficult market; because certainly in the electronics field, if you cannot do business with the government it is pretty hard to survive in the small,

Supply-Industry
restricted consumer market we have in this country. And if the big fellows are going to get all the government business, then it is going to be very difficult for these new industries to develop.
What of industries that are having a difficult time in surviving in the competitive world and yet have something to contribute to Canada's future, and what of the industries we need very badly in times of national crisis? In my constituency there is an industry known as Light Alloys, which is possibly the best foundry in North America manufacturing magnesium castings. During the days when our aircraft industry was thriving, in particular prior to the unhappy demise of the Arrow, this industry was getting along very well. It produces magnesium castings that no other firm in Canada can produce. During the second world war the government was very glad to have that plant and encouraged its development and growth. This was under the leadership of the late C. D. Howe, who I think will go down in history as the man who did more than anyone else to encourage the growth of industry, and in particular the growth of the Canadian aircraft industry in all its allied fields.
Today it is difficult for an industry such as this to compete. It needs encouragement, and possibly some preference from time to time from the government. Ultimately, if industries such as this fold up, we will have to buy these magnesium castings from the United States, and it must be remembered that both the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Trade and Commerce are working very hard to the end that our balance of payments position be improved.
If industries like this are not encouraged to develop, and are not given help at the government level during the difficult years, it may be we will not only lose them as employers but their departure will render great detriment in the field of the international balance of payments.
There is just one other aspect, on which I like to call the social policy, that I believe should concern the department. I suggest there is a great opportunity in the formation of a new department to instil this sort of social philosophy, not only overtly within the department but within the new employees who are coming into it. If they can be made aware there is some national and social purpose to their work and that it is not purely the same as big business, it would be a great help.
In this connection of a social purpose, within the buying rules of the department might I suggest that the minister consider giving a greater preference to Canadian manufacture and production than is presently given. I know it to be a fact that we cannot be national

hogs in this regard. Trade is a two way process, and we cannot set up high barriers to prevent competition. But surely in the area of new industries that we are trying to develop, industries such as electronics, if small industries do not get some protection, the big will surely devour them, and there will be no incentive for our industries to develop. In this regard, in the departmental buying by the old department of defence production I have seen examples of American manufactured goods being bought, goods which did not provide a single job in Canada, and these goods won contracts over goods which were completely manufactured in Canada and which created employment in Canada.
Surely that again redounds to our detriment in the international balance of payments. I wonder if our manufacturers would be permitted to sell on a competitive basis in the defence area in Washington, unless it was under a defence sharing arrangement. I suggest that undoubtedly the American manufacturer gets greater protection in this regard, and surely our Canadian manufacturer, if he is to survive, particularly the new and growing manufacturer, should get some greater preference than is presently given him. I understand our manufacturers are given some preference, but it obviously has not been sufficient to see to it that our defence production contracts go out to as great a degree as possible to those manufacturers and employers who manufacture, and employ men in Canada.
In this regard I would like to bring to the minister's attention one other point. In my sister constituency of North Renfrew is the great atomic energy commission and the plants and works of that organization, which come under the minister's department. It is to be hoped-I think this probably is the case at the present time, and may it continue to be so-that the employees of this organization will be given continued encouragement by way of wages comparable to industry, comparable to what they could obtain in the United States of America, so we may maintain the very favourable and enviable position that we as a small nation have built up in this field. It would be a tragedy indeed if by reason of pettiness or penury at the government payroll stage we in any way impaired this great industry. We have had one sad example of losing so many of our skilled and highly trained aeronautical engineers by reason of the fact that the Arrow is no longer manufactured here. This, an industry in which it had taken years to develop the talents needed, fell apart.
