There is one other point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister with regard to the Department of Industry as it affects my constituents. I suggest that the government plans with regard to the growth and development of our industry have shown a keen concern for the underdeveloped, for the economically unfortunate. I think this is in the best traditions of our party. They have done this in the maritime provinces by giving very large capital funds to assist in the development of this area, which has lagged behind the rest of Canada. They have recognized this principle, an egalitarian principle, if you like, of equalizing opportunity in various parts of Canada, by putting 35 designated areas under the care of the Department of Industry.
Unfortunately, this does not solve all our problems in this regard. I think there are areas of Canada the development of which is very analogous to that of the maritime provinces, but which unfortunately are not physically located in the maritime provinces. There are areas the growth of which has lagged behind, and not over a period of eight years, which was the determining period under the designated areas program-and quite properly so, because the areas that were so designated undoubtedly needed help. These are areas that possibly had grown to a very considerable degree and only lagged behind in the past eight years. I suggest there are areas much as the maritime provinces, even in rich Ontario, which over a period of 50, 75 or 100 years have not kept up with the vast growth in other parts of Ontario and other parts of Canada. Because they were not in the maritime provinces they received no capital grants to help them; and because possibly their lack of growth was not just over eight years, and accordingly they have not had a sudden surge of unemployment-they have been stagnant over many, many more years than eight-there is to date no specific plan to help them. These areas are not slow growth areas under the definition of designated areas, but they need capital help in much the same way that the maritime provinces need capital help.
Supply-Industry
I sincerely trust that the minister in his wisdom will find a way in the new Department of Industry to help this type of area. I suggest this problem is applicable to a considerable part of my constituency and other parts of eastern Ontario, and possibly also to eastern Quebec. They need some sort of capital incentives or, as many of these areas are former lumbering areas that have petered out, perhaps under the Department of Industry it will be found possible to devise some way whereby the remaining lumber resources can be profitably used, with government help and encouragement, to create new industrial hope and new employment.
There is just one other point upon which I should like to touch briefly. It does not particularly affect my constituency, but I think this situation has struck all Canadians from time to time. I refer to the printing bureau. Having read the qualms expressed in the Glassco report about the printing bureau, and having from time to time over many years heard public doubts as to the propriety of having this giant institution doing government printing at the expense of private business, it may be that now this minister has taken over the department and has undoubtedly already shaken it by the heels- which is no doubt a good thing-he will take a look at the entire philosophy behind the printing bureau. Why should government compete to a great degree, as this huge institution does, with private business? If we are going to have a printing bureau competing to this extent, why not start manufacturing cars? I suggest that this is not properly within the government area of business, in a party which embraces private enterprise as its basic philosophy.
We have seen that this bureau publishes myriads and thousands of publications on everything from ducks to cartels. I do not know whether anybody ever reads them. They are undoubtedly published at great public expense. It is very difficult to find the exact cost of the printing bureau under its present set-up. If the set-up indicated in the Glassco report is put into effect and we revamp the fiscal system of the bureau, we may be able to find out exactly what it costs, or at least be able to obtain more accurate figures. There undoubtedly is a place for a government printing bureau, but I think a good look should be taken at it. Are all its publications necessary? Is the taxpayer of Canada paying too much for what he is getting? Are we competing unfairly against small business or private business? We would like the printing bureau to be doing something that is necessary to the government, but not that which is competing unfairly

in the market place and at the same time being the drag on the taxpayer that it appears to be today.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking on these estimates I shall refer to the Department of Industry. This seems to be the most popular department the minister has this evening. The Minister of Industry brought to our attention the fact that a great number of skilled workers, such as scientists, engineers, designers and other professional men were leaving our country to find gainful employment elsewhere. The hon. member for Renfrew South also brought this to our attention a few minutes ago. I should like to ask the minister if he knows the percentage of people leaving Canada because of lack of opportunity here? I think everyone in the house is aware that we are importing many skilled and professional men from outside Canada today.
Will this new department not take the incentive out of industry? The Prime Minister said that this was not a new department and that the facilities for the department would come from the Department of Trade and Commerce. If this the case, why should we have this change? Under the last government the Department of Trade and Commerce was working very successfully and many members of the house realized this. The people of Canada realized it, for in 1961, 1962 and 1963 we experienced the best export trade and business expansion that our country has ever known.
I feel that the setting up of the new Department of Industry could very well mushroom into more and more red tape for our business people. Can the minister tell me whether the staff the new department is employing will come from the Department of National Defence, the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Trade and Commerce or are these people to come from our industries, where I feel they are vitally needed at the present time? If the latter is the case, then since this is a completely new department which will make further demands on industry and labour the result will be that this undoubtedly will be another burden for our industries to carry.
Those who are successful in the manufacturing field do their own planning and are tired of being planned by others. Anyone who has ever been in business knows the enormous amount of paperwork demanded by the government. All these government departments and their demands tend to raise the cost of producing to a point where some businesses find it impossible to continue. Will this department make further demands from

businesses by requesting statistics and reports? I do not believe this is what the Glassco commission recommended. They felt that these departments should be curtailed.
Since the bill has been passed the government has gone over the heads of municipal and provincial authorities to designate depressed areas, and this has caused much unrest and fear in industrial circles throughout the country. The hon. member for Marquette mentioned that this evening. I should like to put on the record an excerpt from an article in the Financial Times this week. It is headed, "Windsor Resents Designated Area Tag" and reads in part as follows:
Greater Windsor has become the federal government's most reluctant ward. It is one of 35 "des-signated areas" in Canada qualifying for special federal assistance because of chronic economic problems. The only trouble is that many in the Windsor area simply do not want the help.
The reason is that, on the surface at least, Windsor and surrounding municipalities have not had it so good for a long time. The economy of the area is largely tied to the fortune of the Canadian auto industry, which is now entering its third boom year in a row. The auto business has been so good, in fact, that Ford and Chrysler have called back men laid off as long as nine years ago. Chrysler has no unemployed men left on any seniority list...
Community officials seem almost obsessed with creating a new image and infusing confidence. But the term "designated area" does not fit into the image-making scheme. Some local officials resent it. They would like the government to withdraw it.
To be fair to the minister I should point out the view of industrial leaders in Windsor.
Industrial leaders do not agree. They think that new industry is more likely to be attracted by the financial benefits of the federal plan than by any new image.
I do not feel that industry in this area should have a preference over industries in other areas. These designated areas were set up before the new Department of Industry was really created and got under way. What can we expect after the new department is completely formed? Industry all across the country is worried. Is the department going to distribute contracts to the favoured industries or to so-called distressed areas? Are they going to affect further the law of supply and demand?
The cost of the new department when it gets rolling will run into millions of dollars. My chief question is, does industry need this guidance? I should like to ask the minister this question: Will any assistance be given to universities to set up research departments to aid industry, so that these services would be available for the development of new products and new methods of manufacuring? By promoting this type of research in our universities we would be setting up a challenge to the students and making available

information to industry that I feel is not available at the present time.
Finally, I should like to say that we must find markets and capital for industry. If we find these I am sure industry will build and expand in Canada without too much assistance from this new department.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about the Department of Industry and the problems we in Canada face at this stage in our economic development. Some feel, like the previous speaker and other speakers, that our development should be haphazard. There is a happy go lucky theory that everything good is going to come to Canada, that there are unused frontiers and all we have to do is go west and the untapped virgin resources will pay for all our problems and all our mistakes, and that somehow or other the inevitable destiny of Canada is up, up and up ascending plateaus. I feel this is not realistic economics. It is not a realistic examination of the economic problems that face Canada in the sixties.
One needs only to look at the rate of economic expansion in countries which we always considered old hat. Somehow or other Italy was poor, Britain was in another century, France had its grandeur in other days and Germany was destroyed. If you take a look at the rate of economic development in these countries during the past decade you will see that it far exceeded the rate of growth in Canada, and far exceeded the rate of growth in the United States. Rich as we are in natural resources, abundant as we are in the things required to make economic growth, countries like Italy, poor in economic resources, have shown a much higher rate of growth.
Industrial activity in the north of Italy was so great that it was necessary to import labour from other countries into the rural areas of the south to replace those attracted by growth in the north. The rate of German recovery has been phenomenal. The skilled labour in Germany, plus the stream of refugees from the east and the great torrents of United States capital which were invested there after the war made for enormous economic development. France is a country which has surged ahead. Somehow or other it became one of the household fixtures in North America that France periodically would be involved in great crises. The franc was in a constant process of devaluation. Yet we have this enormous industrial expansion in France. France is a rich country, and has reached economic maturity with policies adequate to the circumstances of today.
We always looked to Britain in the latter years to face crisis after crisis. They have 28902-5-338
Supply-Industry
had problems of exchange and yet the British economy has bounded ahead. These things did not occur by happenstance. These things did not come about because somehow or other the month of the calendar arrived and that was the month to go ahead. A proper assessment was taken of the problems of these countries. They marshalled their resources and made a plan and encouraged the development of their economies along productive and economic lines.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this country has reached the end of its frontier. We can no longer look for boundless discoveries of natural resources that are somehow or other going to pay our bills. We have to make a proper assessment of our capabilities; we have to take a proper inventory of our resources. We must take a look at our manpower, we must measure our markets and we must plan to assure that Canada will achieve ascending plateaus in economic development.
The history of Canada has been from staples to highly processed commodities. We all know that Canada started with the fishing industry, the cod on the east coast, the lumbering industry and the fur trade which hammered out the frontiers of the land. It was wheat and lumber and all our staples, which measured the economic development of the country.
Now we are in a period of industrial growth. We went into the first war with about half of our labour force employed in agriculture. After two world wars we have become very highly mechanized and industrialized. Today the portion of our labour force engaged in agriculture is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 11 or 12 per cent. Today we find that 26 per cent of our labour force is employed by industry, and 26 per cent of our production comes from industry. It is interesting to see what is happening with industry, because it is facing a serious testing time. We have to take the measure of our secondary industries and see what we can do by way of mobilizing our best resources, which I believe this department can and is most likely to do, in order to assist in the planning of our economic and industrial growth. Twenty six per cent of the value of all goods and services produced in Canada are produced by industry. Industry also accounts for 26 per cent of our employment. Since 1945 there has been an increase of only 15.6 per cent in the labour force in industry, but an increase of 61.2 per cent in our volume of production. That means that more and more industry is becoming highly mechanized, more efficient, and production is growing. We must mobilize our

Supply-Industry
resources to ensure that we can use highly efficient industry to engage the manpower of the country.
There is the enormous importance of capital investment as the key to the rate of economic growth. If we do not have a sufficient rate of capital investment, then we will not have an adequate rate of growth to use our plants and employ our manpower. We are increasing the rate of capital investment. It slowed down in the early 1960's but is increasing again. We are once more enjoying a high rate of economic growth. As industry expands and the rate of industrial production grows, and investment flows into industry, there is an increase to new plateaus.
I should now like to say a word about the training of our labour force. We have to invest in industry, we have to invest in factories, we have to invest in arterial roads, and all the paraphernalia of industrial development. But we also have to invest in men. A few days ago we discussed a new bill to increase facilities for training manpower. It seems to me that the training of manpower for industry must be associated with industry, not only with formal education. Formal education quite often puts handicaps in the way of absorbing people into the training stream, because we place restrictions on those who can be trained, on who can qualify for industrial training in schools of formal education. They have to have a certain standard of formal education to begin with. We are bringing to this country hundreds of thousands of people who will never be absorbed into our formal schools of education. We must expand facilities for on-job training, and we must examine the plans in Europe which have led the way to on-job training to increase industrial skills, and to investment in manpower.
Another thing we must look at is management. Robert Macaulay, a recent minister of industry in Ontario, made a sensational speech in the city of Windsor the other day in which he said the management in this country is not moving ahead or meeting the challenge, and that it is not as developed as it might be. The problem of management is something we must look at to ensure that we get the most efficient and wisest direction of industry.
Now, Mr. Chairman, a good deal has been said about foreign capital in this country. I sympathize very much with those concerned about the control of industry, but I feel that the problem of foreign capital is an economic one. It is not a political problem, as has been said; it is primarily an economic problem. It is an economic problem to the extent that we have to pay a price in foreign exchange for foreign capital investment in this country. To the extent that we can pay that price
[Mr. Gelber.l
we should do so. We must welcome capital investment and make it profitable. We should create conditions which are profitable and secure for all people who invest in this country. At the point where the price becomes too onerous we must look at the problem, and I believe we have to do more to encourage investment by Canadians in Canadian industry. Foreign industry has brought to this country great know-how and industrial skills, both in management and in labour. It is a debt we will have to continue to pay, and to which we must look and remember. Not only have many of the people who have migrated to this country come here highly skilled, but the branch plants which have been established by the most advanced and mature industries of the world have brought their skills, their techniques, their understanding and their knowledge of markets for developing Canadian industry.
We must plan, Mr. Chairman, and put our best intelligence to this problem. It presents many challenges to Canada in the 1960's. I believe the minister and his able assistant will give a direction and an understanding, which will bring a formulation of policies and lend incentives, so that Canada can continue to grow and use her best industrial might for the welfare of all.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Department of Industry provide an opportunity to say a few words on this newly-created department. It has been created by an act of parliament and includes not only its new sphere but also several departments or branches of departments which were already in existence. Above all we want new industry. I am one who is hoping that the new Department of Industry will turn in a good account of itself. We are doing everything possible to assist the minister in the riding of Macleod and in the Crowsnest pass, which has been designated a slow growth area, in order to bring about industrial development.
Before coming to some of the things we are doing by way of co-operation with this department I should like to bring to the attention of the minister some of the obstacles facing his department. There has been some criticism of the word "industry" as the name of the new department. I do not wish to go into the pros and cons, but I think everyone realizes there has been a certain amount of public criticism of the choice of that particular word. I have also heard it said-and I have no hesitation about mentioning this; I do so for a purpose-that a number of industrialists are somewhat afraid that this new department will be in a position where certain individuals may be able to dictate to

them. I hope the minister and the splendid officials he now has from one end of his department to the other will exercise caution in their dealings with industry, and be very careful at all times not to take any kind of dictatorial attitude toward industry. I think, on the other hand, that the policy of the department must be spelled out. It must be made clear and set down in such a way as to enable all those who wish to work with the department or to take advantage of the offers to be able to do so without the possibility of misunderstanding.
The other day, speaking on the estimates of the Department of Finance, I raised the question of the 95 per cent new machinery requirement imposed on new industry desiring to take advantage of the designated area assistance. I still hope the minister will reconsider this particular provision, if he has not already done so. If he has some change to announce in this regard I would be delighted to hear him. I would point out that when small industries are being started in the new area it is usual for them to gather together machinery which has already been used and move into premises which are not new. A great deal of capital is necessary before a new industry can become established, and it is often necessary to begin by using second hand machinery and buildings which have been occupied before. I was hopeful when I raised this question with the Minister of Finance that he would be able to make some alteration in this rigid rule with respect to the 95 per cent requirement.
In the Crowsnest pass area we have the only designated area in Alberta. Part of it is in Alberta and lies within the Macleod riding, but the western part of the designated area lies within the constituency of east Kootenay. The area in Alberta has already organized a chamber of commerce which includes the entire Crowsnest pass area. In other words, instead of having a chamber of commerce attached to each particular town, we have one body for the entire area. In addition, the people there have organized an association known as the Crowsnest pass development association. They have gone several steps beyond that. They asked the Oldman river regional planning commission to help by preparing a new brochure which will bring together all the potentialities for industrial development, and make them available to prospective investors who might wish to know what the opportunities are in the Crowsnest pass area. The feeling is one of optimism. We	have	seen a
tremendous growth of industrial development in southwestern Alberta during the past six or seven years. Some 20 new industries have been started in the Macleod riding. And 28902-5-338i

I might spend a few moments pointing out how some of these industries that we now have came about. One method has been the sale of abandoned airports. The airport at Macleod was sold to the town of Fort Macleod, and the town in turn resold two hangars to a plywood manufacturing concern which is now employing over 60 people. When it is in full swing we expect it will employ over 100 people. The other hangars were sold to a trailer manufacturing concern which is employing between 60 and 70 people. Then a steel factory was established in another hangar and this, in turn, has been employing 30 or 40 people. The Trail Smelters, selling fertilizer, have purchased one hangar and have put in a spur railroad. They are now employing 20 or 30 people and using the hangar as a warehouse and distribution point for Elephant brand fertilizer. Another hangar has been leased to a furniture and mattress manufacturing concern.
So industries are coming to the old town of Fort Macleod. It stood still for a number of years but now, with the sale of the airport and the spread of industry there, everything is booming. The people are happy and that is what we want to see all over, with the growth and development of new industry.
The Vulcan airport was sold to the county of Vulcan and the county, in turn, sold part of it to a concern which is building houses. I understand this concern is now doing very well. I am informed by the minister, by officials of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, by members of the municipality of Willow Creek and of the town of Claresholm that the sale of the Claresholm airport is in its final stages, if it has not been completed. I made the suggestion to the three levels of government that they should get together and decide among themselves on the purchase of this airport. The purchase has been held up for a number of years as a result of legal action, but this was all swept away with the amendment of the Alberta municipal district act. It was hoped that these three levels of government would formulate a policy which, in turn, would help the industrialization of the Claresholm area.
While I am on this subject I want to say a word of congratulation and thanks to the people in the Department of Industry and in particular to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. During the past five years I have had occasion, during the handling of these other airports, to co-operate with and do my part as a member to help bring about this development of industry in these old

We have had word, Mr. Chairman, of this terrible new tragedy, this airplane tragedy, which occurred between Montreal and Toronto in which 111 passengers and seven crew members were involved, and this has served to dampen our whole evening performance. There is a bigger crowd out in the rotunda than there is in this chamber. This tragedy brings to one's mind the question of safety, which is an industrial problem. These airplanes are manufactured in Canada, the United States or in England. Safety is of paramount importance in the construction of these airplanes in this day and age, when we look to air travel as one of the accepted methods of travel.
So, Mr. Chairman, I close with the hope that the Department of Industry, with the problems which a new department does have, will be able to overcome the difficulties with which they are faced. Finally, I should like to invite the minister to come to the west, and I will take him in a car to the Crows-nest pass and show him what we have in the way of natural resources that we want developed. We want more petrochemical industries. We have almost every natural resource you can imagine, but what we need is industry. We have 7 per cent of the world's coal supply, and we believe that industries which locate in the area will be competitive with those operated in any other area of Canada. So, I extend an invitation to the minister to visit us and become familiar with the things that we have to offer. Then, as a result of this close-up view he will be in a better position to appraise the work of his department and co-operate with all of us who are trying to co-operate with him.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a few words to the remarks made today on the estimates of the Department of Defence Production and of the new Department of Industry, in order to comment on certain events likely to influence the economic growth of our country, and more especially of some of its areas.
I know that the new Department of Industry, headed by the hon. member for St.

Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Drury), who is also Minister of Defence Production, is a department which in the next months and in future years will become vitally important if our country is to undergo the industrial development which we all hope for and which our country sorely needs.
Mr. Chairman, if we wish to direct the development of industry and of our natural resources, I think that the Department of Industry which has just been established along with the Canada economic council will have an essential part to play. However, its function will be conditioned by the co-operation granted by the provincial governments and other similar bodies which these authorities have established to look after the development of our natural resources.
Mr. Chairman, this shows our need of a liaison body between the provincial and federal authorities, in order to develop our industries and our natural resources.
We cannot imagine at the present time the federal government fully discharging its duties without a close and continuous co-operation with the provincial governments. I believe the discussions which have taken place these last few days, within the framework of the federal-provincial conference just ended, have proved that we could no longer conceive the role of the federal government as an absolute one to be played regardless of the needs and wishes of the provinces.
I believe that, in the economic development of our country, we must not expect any action to achieve concrete results without the full co-operation of provincial organizations.
Mr. Chairman, many recent developments in our country were such as to make us understand how important that co-operation is.
I should like to refer especially to what happened when an attempt was being made to designate the areas in this country which were to get special assistance from the government to deal with chronic and permanent unemployment.
From what we have heard, those areas were designated without the provincial governments being consulted beforehand.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that this shows the extent of the lack of co-operation and planning.
The provincial governments have area development agencies and economic planning agencies. When the central government decides to choose arbitrarily some areas in order to help them, without taking into account the views expressed or the plans submitted by the provincial governments, I think that proves the lack of co-operation which must necessarily result in duplication

of agencies that must help an area. I do not think that is in the interest of our country and its expansion.
These designated areas were selected according to criteria referring to the unemployment situation over the last eight years. I know that several criticisms were submitted to the various departments concerned as well as to the Minister of Industry, about the basis which was used for the selection of these areas.
Like many other members, I submitted my personal criticisms and those of my fellow citizens on this matter, precisely because some criteria that were used as a basis were not fair and did not represent the problem as it existed.
I know that other areas and other cities were designated since, and can benefit from the advantages of the plan. And I am sure also that here again we have a measure that is only a temporary makeshift to the major problem which faces us at this time, namely the development of our industries.
As most hon. members in the house and probably most citizens in this country, I followed with interest the effort made by the Minister of Industry to increase the production of automobile parts in our country.
Mr. Chairman, I was surprised at a certain moment to see that Canadian ministers had to go to the United States in order to request, or rather to beg permission to increase production of automobile parts in Canada. I then realized to what extent we were dependent on the United States and also to what extent we were still a colony. I realized how impossible it is to understand that Canada is politically independent, since, at the base of all independence, there must be economic independence, and there is no possible sovereignty, if we do not have first of all economic independence. I was really amazed to see that we had to ask the Americans permission to increase our production of parts involved in the construction of automobiles used on Canadian roads.
That leads me into believing

I may be wrong-that if the Canadian government saw fit to choose the DC-9 for T.C.A. rather than another aircraft, no matter where it came from, but which would have been practically completely built in Canada, that decision was taken under undue pressure. Indeed, the aircraft chosen is still in the development stage and the government probably reached that decision in order to be authorized, in return, to increase production of automobile parts in Canada.
We know that the American government, through some of its high officials, threatened to retaliate to that praiseworthy project of
Supply-Industry
the minister, which I completely approve, to increase production of automobile parts in Canada. I think that the minister and probably the government had to make some concession behind the curtains to get the authorization to increase production of automobile parts in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, that was very detrimental to our country because if we must, every time we wish to increase our industrial production in this country, concede an advantage in the same proportion to another sector of the American industry, all our efforts are useless and give no concrete or practical result.
I understand, Mr. Chairman, that the government based its decision on technical reports prepared by experts who picked the DC-9 rather than the Caravelle or another aircraft. It simply played with words, because this same government rejected the findings of the report submitted by these same experts to keep the maintenance depot of Trans-Canada Air Lines in Winnipeg.
There we see to what extent a government may be influenced first by political considerations and secondly by unwarranted pressures from a foreign power on our industrial development. We, of the central government, want to use the whole potential of this country to increase its productivity, to fight unemployment in the various sectors, and I suggest this is quite fair and normal. The Department of Industry and especially that of defence production, which are both under the same man, should realize that the country is made up of ten provinces, when the time comes to award contracts to meet the requirements of the Department of National Defence concerning armaments or various supplies.
Thus, in those contracts to be awarded, the lowest tender should not be the only factor to consider. Keeping the economic development of our country in proper balance should also be taken into account. By that, I want to point out to the minister that when, in any one year, he has to grant contracts to the amount of about $100 million, the provinces are entitled to consideration on a fair basis for these contracts. No province has a priority right.
I hope the minister will remember that there are in the province of Quebec, as well as in the province of Ontario and other provinces in Canada, industries which are duly qualified to meet the needs of his department. Moreover, such a policy would help reduce the high level of unemployment we now have in the province of Quebec.

speechtext: Five years will take us to 1968. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext: I suggest that the tripling of support in relation to the hon. member's forecast of only a doubling of enrolment indicates that there will be a relative increase in support. As I indicated, we do recognize that more has to be done. In the forecast I have just given of a rate that is triple perhaps recognition should be had of the fact that, as the hon. member pointed out a little while ago, one of our tasks is not only to increase the output of the universities but more particularly to find jobs for them in Canada. The hon. member will recollect the figure that he gave, that some 26 per cent of those who graduated went elsewhere than Canada to find work. It seems to me, as I indicated in my initial remarks, that the first and increasing emphasis should be placed on increasing the possibilities of these graduates in the physical sciences finding employment within Canada, while at the same time increasing the scale of assistance itself. All I can say is that we have a slightly different scale of priority than that suggested by the hon. member for Port Arthur. But I would indicate that the national research council intends to increase its support to universities in light of the measure of its present effort and the forecast expansion of our universities.
